The Authority of Scripture;
dedicated to establishing the authority of the Śrī Pañcarātra Tantra;
[composed] by the supreme teacher of the venerable Bhāṣyakāras.
Composed by the venerable Śrī Yāmunācārya Svāmin;
edited in certain difficult passages by Paṇḍita Svāmi Śrī Rāmamiśra Śāstrin, a teacher of the true tradition and one who is independent in all systems of thought.
And it has been elucidated by the Paramaguru of Śrībhāṣyācārya.
Edited by Śrī Rāmeśvara Pāṭhaka at Vārāṇasī; printed at the Tārā Press.
In the year 1994 of the Vikrama era; 1937 CE. Śrīḥ!
Salutation to Śrī. Salutation to the Lord of Śrī.
Salutation to the illustrious Rāmānuja.
Salutations again and again to Yāmuna, salutations again and again;
salutations again and again to Yāmuna, salutations again and again.
In whom the ancient words here find their ultimate purpose—

Victorious forever is this noble sage Rāmānuja, the pilot of the ship for crossing the ocean of worldly existence; he effects the destruction of grief for those who have fainted from being deceived by various [worldly objects].
Śrī, obeisance to Śrī; obeisance to Śrīdhara.
Salutations to the Blessed Yāmunamuni;
salutations to the venerable Rāmānuja.

The *Āgamaprāmāṇya* composed by the venerable Ācārya Mādhyamandāra (Mādhava): Salutations to Viṣṇu, the sole cause of the birth, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe, who perceives the entire world as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of his hand.
Let those few men who, out of envy, are of similar age yet possess evil minds, disparage this speech—though it is profound and endowed with merit; let them disparage it.
There are many virtuous people who, having reached the further shore of the state of skill in discerning the essential from the non-essential,
are free from envy and praise my words.
Error may arise even for those of great learning whose minds are dominated by dogmatic attachment;
therefore, let the wise here, free from envy, reflect upon this doctrine of the Bhāgavata.
In this regard, some—

whose minds have been conquered by the surging froth of various petty sophistries they have gathered here and there— display their own extraordinary skill in critical inquiry under the pretext of protecting the path of the Triple Veda (Trayī).
They disagree regarding the authority of the Pañcarātra-tantras, which have as their object the unsurpassed supreme beatitude (niḥśreyasa) fashioned by the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa);
and they say:
Indeed, the validity of words is determined to be twofold:
one depends on another means of knowledge, while the other is independent.
In that regard as well:
A statement whose composition is dependent upon a person never attains the status of a means of valid cognition, which is characterized by independence.
For human speech,

when employed to present an object already apprehended by another means of valid cognition, attains the status of a valid means of knowledge only by conforming to the speaker's realization of that object.

Nor does it [the Veda] establish the relationship between the means and the ends— such as heaven or liberation— which are desired, preceded by an initiation (*dīkṣā*) distinct from that prescribed in the *Pañcarātra-tantras*, and consisting of the worship of the Blessed Lord.

Perception and the other means of knowledge are capable of making things known; for we do not, by perceiving initiation, ritual service, and so forth through direct perception, come to understand their status as means for attaining the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).

Furthermore, there is no evidence that any recent individuals possessing superhuman powers have directly perceived these [scriptures] as being a means to achieve their desired ends; for even their sense organs, such as the eyes and so forth, [are limited].
It is not possible to transcend the nature of the sense-faculties as they are perceived.
But is it not observed that direct perception varies according to the difference in its basis?
Therefore, it certainly comes to final rest in some substratum as its support.

For everything that possesses gradation is seen to reach a state of non-gradation, just as dimension [reaches its limit] in space; and since such gradation is directly observed among crows, owls, vultures, and others, it stands to reason that this [knowledge] must also be so. And this is the case for knowledge...
The ultimate limit is that which has everything as its object; for in this world, cognitions excel one another precisely by virtue of having a wider range of objects.
It is the same with qualities such as sovereignty, dispassion, and power.
The wise maintain that there exist in some person those qualities from which all excellence has been cast away.
Therefore,

it is the Blessed One himself— who possesses this direct perception that directly perceives the various states of existence supporting all these worlds, and who has realized the nature of dharma such as initiation and its cultivation— who explains it thus.
"What is impossible about this? To that we reply: Even if you were to postulate an excellence in perceptual cognition, it would not be capable of transcending its own object-domain to grasp another.
For instance:
"In the case of color and that which inheres in the same object as color,
it is logical that there should be an excellence [of perception], just like the excellence observed [in other cases]."
Thus, while the consciousness of another sense organ might take the universe as its object,
how could perceptual consciousness be capable of cognizing the universe?
But surely, its capacity has been established for the apprehension of what exists;

for if there were no apprehension of what exists— which is necessarily connected to its own nature— then perception itself would be overturned, since that which is unborn or past [cannot be perceived].

Or, if one were to bring inference and the like under the category of perception, then the excellence of perception—characterized by having all things as its object—would have its arising uprooted by the constraints of its own nature; thus, this [position] does not find favor with the heart. This also [is the case].

Inferring the unsurpassed from that which possesses degrees of excellence, you should explain when questioned: "Does that which possesses excellence itself ever reach such a state that no further greatness can possibly exist beyond it?
You are clinging to this like a child imagining the state of old age.
Now, regarding that which is superior in one respect, must it be surpassed by something else that is absolutely unsurpassed,
or rather, must it reach a state of absolute unsurpassability through another of the same kind?
The first alternative is not tenable because it is unperceived;
for a vessel or the like is never seen to have attained the vastness of space.
And if that very [pot] were to reach a state of excellence so unsurpassable that no further height could be conceived, alas! then every single pot, jar,
and the like would fill the entire interior cavity of the cosmic egg.
Because its very opposition entails the collapse of all other entities,
the middle [reason] is a *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established), since it has attained its probandum by means of space itself; furthermore,
even under another interpretation, the previously mentioned refutation remains unavoidable.
Indeed, no excellence has ever been seen before in which a pillar extending to the end of a pillar of Vibhu exists; likewise, that very contradiction remains established.
Furthermore, even that measurement demonstrated here in the sky must indeed be examined;
for "measurement" (parimāṇa) means delimitation by space, that is to say, a finite extent or being encompassed on all sides.
And since that [quality] does not exist in space, how can it be indicated here as an illustration?

Furthermore, if one were to infer that quality in space, even then, because its supreme excellence would be merely a possibility, there would again be the fallacy of the example being devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).

Nor is there any evidence that initiation (*dīkṣā*), ritual service (*ārādhanā*), and so forth, have been cognized as *dharma* by means of some extraordinary perception; therefore, the postulation of an excess of another's consciousness that has not been observed by us and others is minimal.

Perception is not a valid means of knowledge regarding the relationship between the intended object of proof and its means of accomplishment; much less, therefore, can the *Pañcarātra* Smṛti be a valid authority based upon it.
Furthermore, there can be no invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with respect to the subject at hand, which lies far beyond the path of the senses.

Inference is capable of arising only when dependent upon mental retention (*dhāraṇā*); for those who have never experienced fire do not connect smoke with it through the relation of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). Nor can scripture establish the necessity of performing the collection of rites established by the *Sāttvata* tradition.
An author is not perceived, by virtue of whom the *Pañcarātra* Smṛtis might be authoritative on the grounds of having him as their source;
nor is he, though unperceived, an object of inference, just as [the author of the Tantras is not], for instance,
in the case of the means and ends consisting of initiation (*dīkṣā*), ritual worship (*rādhanā*) well-known in the Tantras, and the desired results such as heaven (*svarga*).

An existent entity (*bhāva*) is not within the scope of inference because of the absence of a determined relationship; likewise, the scripture (*āgama*) rooted in that [inference] cannot be inferred for the same reason. Nor can the scripture that serves as the basis for the memory under discussion be understood through scripture alone.
For that [cognition] arises in two ways, through the distinction between human and non-human [speech].
First of all, its occurrence does not arise from human speech,
because humans might even speak what is false for the sake of deception.
For even today, some who consider themselves wise are seen explaining non-scriptural matters under the guise of scripture.

In this regard, is the claim that their own compositions are rooted in the Veda made by the authors of the Pañcarātra texts preceded by an understanding of the Āgamas which constitute their foundation, or is it merely for the sake of persuasion on the part of those who compose according to their own whims?
We suspect that such is the case with their statement;
and by that much, the intended validity [of their scripture] would be contradicted,
for there exists no eternal scripture (nityāgama) whose object is of such a nature.
Nor can that [Vedic] source-text be established through analogy, because it is impossible;
for how could that [text], never before perceived, become the object of a cognition based on similarity?

Nor can that root Śruti be established through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), because there is no logical inconsistency [otherwise]. For the postulation of such a text arises only from the fact that memory would otherwise be inexplicable. Indeed, the authors of the Pañcarātra remember [their own teachings], such as initiation and ritual worship, as being dharma, just as they do the Aṣṭakā and other rites.
Manu and others [are the authors].
Furthermore, the capacity for recollection does not manifest with respect to an object that has not been experienced;
and experience is preceded by sense organs, logical marks, verbal testimony, similarity, or an otherwise inexplicable fact.
In such a case, since experience does not manifest from other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it postulates *codanā* alone as its source;

thus, this intention of the mind might indeed be established, provided that the restriction of experiences to being in accordance with reality were itself validated by a means of valid cognition. However, when...

Furthermore, for those whose internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa) are governed by attachment, aversion, dogmatic adherence, and so forth, meditations conditioned by unreal experiences produce corresponding memories; how then, in the absence of such recollection, could the authoritative scripture (śruti) be postulated?
Since remembrance can be accounted for in other ways as well, what is to be said regarding the remembrances of Manu and others?
But surely the arguments previously stated apply there too; for indeed, the notion that the Aṣṭakā is a means to achieve a desired end does not arise in those who have merely witnessed it.

Nor is it inference, because no connection [between the two] is perceived; nor is it verbal testimony, because that [word] is not apprehended; nor can what is unapprehended be inferred, precisely because no connection is perceived; nor is it an object of comparison, because no similar thing can be identified; nor is it...
It is possible to postulate [a Vedic text], because it was just mentioned that the occurrence of memory otherwise is possible;
for there is no possibility of the memory of a person who has a connection with the Veda.
If a Śruti is postulated in this case, then let it be postulated elsewhere as well.
For even in the Pañcarātra, the supreme sages headed by Nārada and Śāṇḍilya are remembered as the originators of the tradition.

And therefore: Since the objections and their resolutions are equal, both the Pañcarātra and the Manusmṛti would be either authoritative or non-authoritative; a distinction between them is not logical.

Either let the status of being an authoritative source regarding the Smṛtis of Manu and others be abandoned, or else the specific distinction of the Pañcarātra must be stated; that [distinction] is now being stated.
Alternatively, by formulating the sūtra "it is a means of valid knowledge because of the identity of the agent," the author of the sūtras has made clear the intended distinction.
For instance, [this applies] to the rites prescribed by Śruti, such as the Agnihotra, the Darśapūrṇamāsa, and the Jyotiṣṭoma,
as well as to the rites prescribed by Smṛti, such as the Aṣṭakā, the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana).

Because it was taught by their fathers and others, the three classes of elders learned in the three Vedas are seen to perform its practice without distinction, out of the conviction that it is supremely beneficial; therefore,
by virtue of the firm acceptance of such cultured members of the three classes, [the Veda is established as authoritative].

The cognition of the duties to be performed, such as the Aṣṭakā, which are clearly perceived, relies upon the Veda itself as its foundational source, for that [Veda] is most capable of establishing them.
And it is not the case that this is like [the knowledge of] sipping water (ācamana), initiation (upanayana), and so forth.
We observe those who perform the ritual acts of the Agnihotra and other rites prescribed by the Śruti, yet practice the Tantric customs;
on the contrary, the proponents of the Vedas censure them for doing so.
Therefore, that which was stated regarding the authority of the Smṛtis on the grounds of their having the same author—
That [system], such as the Pañcarātra and others, does not deserve to be considered a traditional Smṛti of outsiders;
for the learned of the three higher castes do not practice the matters taught therein.

Now, even in that case, since the practice is performed daily by Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇas who wear the topknot, the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), and so forth as prescribed by Śruti and Smṛti, how can its basis in Vedic injunction (*codanāmūlatva*) not be possible?
It is argued that errors, deceptions, and the like, which are the opposites of validity,
are postulated as the causes of memory. To this, it is replied:

Ah! Thus speaking, you have effectively established the authority [of our position], namely, that the Bhāgavatas are the true refined ones (śiṣṭas), while those who hate the three higher castes are not.
[Objection: But how can they be unrefined when they are Brahmins, the foremost among the three social classes? [Reply:

That is not so; they do not even possess the status of belonging to the three classes, let alone the status of being Brahmins, for [the capacity for knowledge] does not arise immediately upon the contact of the senses in certain specific bodies alone.
We perceive a specific caste-distinction called "Brahminhood" as something distinct from mere humanity, which persists through various stages while excluding others;
however, the topknot, the sacred thread, and so forth, which are prescribed for Brahmins and the like, are not [such].
They are neither capable of producing that state [of the word] nor of making it understood,
because deviation is observed in the case of wicked Śūdras and others; therefore,
the undisputed usage of elders (*vṛddha*) alone is the cause of comprehension here.

Furthermore, worldly people do not employ the term "brāhmaṇa" for the Bhāgavatas without hesitation; rather, there is a designation by way of distinction: "the Brāhmaṇas are here, the Bhāgavatas are there. This might be argued: [that the term applies] to Brāhmaṇas themselves due to the connection with some particular quality.
The claim that the designations "Sāttvata," "Bhāgavata," and so forth are like the terms "parivrājaka" and others applied to those very same [groups] is not correct;
for by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), the word "Sāttvata" refers to certain people of low birth.
It is said that when these [factors] exist, this word functions; it does not apply elsewhere.
Those who know the principles of reasoning maintain that it is improper to accept the etymological (yoga) power of a word in opposition to its conventional (rūḍhi) power,
as in the case of the term *rathakāra*;
for otherwise, how could [the rule] be so?

The word *rathakāra*, even by abandoning its etymological application— which would otherwise involve a breach of the status of being a limb of knowledge established through study— settles upon a specific caste. And there exist certain people called Sātvatas, who are of low birth, descended from Vaiśya-vrātyas, and are devoid of the purificatory rites such as initiation (*upanayana*).
As Manu has said:
"From a Vaiśya Vratya are born the Sudhanvan, the Ācārya, the Bhāruṣa,
the Nijaṅgha, the Maitra, and the Sātvata."
Thus,
there is no dispute here that the word *bhāgavata* is applied to the Sātvatas.
And they remember:
"The fifth is named Sātvata; he who worships the abodes of Viṣṇu by the command of kings is remembered as a Bhāgavata. Thus it is said.
Likewise, they remember this very [practice] as a means of livelihood resulting from the birth of those declared *vrātya*;
for these people are seen here visibly performing it for the sake of their livelihood. And thus Uśanas says:
"For all [castes], living by agriculture and weapons; for the teacher and the Sāttvata, the worship of the gods."
"Likewise, in the Brāhma [Purāṇa]: 'By the command of the kings, he shall worship the ancient shrines of Viṣṇu';
and likewise elsewhere: 'The purification of the temples of the Sātvatas, the purification of the food offerings (naivedya), and the protection of the images. Likewise...
To dispel such a doubt, the words of Manu state:
"Whether they are hidden or manifest, they are to be known by their own actions."
Moreover, their non-Brahminhood is evident from their conduct:
their ritual practice consists of the worship of deities, initiation, and the consumption of sacrificial offerings.
The performance of other sacraments beginning with conception and ending with cremation,
the non-performance of Vedic rites, and the avoidance of association with the twice-born.
Through such improper conducts as these, the loss of Brahminhood is easily determined;
for they remember that [such conduct] is the cause of disqualification from the worship of the gods and from the duties of a Brahmin, just as [they do for other acts].
"For those whose [right to perform] worship of the deity arises solely from the lineage succession, they lack the qualification for Vedic study, for sacrificing, or for officiating at sacrifices.
And likewise, in the *Paramasaṃhitā*:
Their very words are as follows:
"Even in the midst of dire calamity, whether out of fear or being destitute,
one should never worship the God of gods for the sake of a livelihood."

Furthermore, even their practice of wearing the remains of offerings (nirmālya) from all kinds of distinguished and censured deities, as well as consuming the sacrificial food (naivedya), serves only to manifest their lack of Brahminhood.

Moreover, we consider how the acceptance [of these practices] implies a basis in the Śruti, given that even for acts such as looking at [the sun], they prescribe specific penances like the Cāndrāyaṇa; for they indeed record [this in their Smṛtis]: [They] remember: ... (as per the source text) ... Thus, we conclude that their authority must ultimately rest upon the Veda.

Regarding the expiation for visiting *devalakas* (temple-attendants): these *devalakas* are so called because they subsist on the property of the deity (*devakośa*) and perform worship of the deity for the sake of their livelihood. Thus says Devala:
"He who subsists on the property of the deity is called a *devalaka*."
Likewise, that twice-born man who worships the deity for the sake of a livelihood is indeed called a *devalaka*, and he is censured in all ritual acts.
Thus it is said.
Furthermore, these [people] are seen to propitiate the gods solely for the sake of their livelihood through the succession of their lineages; therefore—
Even against one's will, the status of a temple-attendant (devalaka) must be acknowledged as such; and accordingly:
"A Brahmin, while eating, shall not look at a village pig, a eunuch, a sacrificial post, a temple-attendant, or a corpse; having seen any of these, he should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."
Thus they record the penance;
and likewise Atri describes their status as being even more clearly [inferior] to that of the Upabrāhmaṇas:
"The Devalakas who do not possess sand, the Kalpadevalakas, the Gaṇabhogadevalakas, and those whose livelihood is that of the Bhāgavatas."

The fourth [category] consists of these so-called *upabrāhmaṇas*, as the Blessed Vyāsa has stated: "Those who summon [for sacrifices], those who live off the gods (*devalakas*), those who sacrifice for constellations or villages,
and fifthly, long-distance travelers— these are the *caṇḍālas* among Brahmins."

Thus, in this way, the very fact that the followers of the Bhāgavata path have fallen away from the threefold Vedic path (trayīmārga) by virtue of their birth and their actions is sufficient as a reason to reject the authority of the Pañcarātra scriptures; for it is thus.
The Tantra under dispute is not a valid authority regarding merit and demerit,
because it is accepted by those outside the Vedic tradition, just like the statement concerning the worship of a caitya.

Moreover, they themselves proclaim through their own words that their instruction of all dharmas is preceded by the abandonment of the path of the Three Vedas— such as "Having not obtained the supreme good in the four Vedas,
Śāṇḍilya studied this scripture," and so forth; how then can this be [consistent]?

One might conjecture that, by setting aside the idea that even the four Vedas provide knowledge of the means to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), [the author] begins [this work] by declaring that the meaning understood through their grace is itself the human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
For Manu and others are seen declaring that the sole root of the entire collection of means for achieving every desired goal they intend to teach is the scripture:
"The Veda is the root of all Dharma, as are the Smṛti and the conduct of those who know it."

"Dharma is that which is prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti; all of that is declared in the Veda, for it consists of all knowledge. And furthermore: "For those who have been consecrated by the initiatory rite (upanayana) and are thus qualified..."

Furthermore, the description of the purificatory rite (saṃskāra) characterized as initiation (dīkṣā), for the sake of establishing eligibility for the worship of the Lord in all Vedic rites such as the Agnihotra, only imitates its non-Vedic nature; for if it were truly Vedic, [it would not require such a justification].
By those very same saṃskāras, they would also be entitled to the worship of the Blessed One and other such rites.

Furthermore, their non-inclusion among the fourteen branches of knowledge (vidyāsthāna) accepted by all orthodox believers as authoritative sources for dharma is also an indicative mark (liṅga) of their non-Vedic nature.

Otherwise, this too would be remembered as one of those [other systems]; yet it is not so remembered. Therefore, it is determined that this recollection of the Pañcarātra is indeed non-Vedic. For this very reason, by the venerable Bādarāyaṇa...

The refutation of this system occurs on the occasion of rejecting the heterodox collections (*bāhyasamaya*), such as those of Kaṇabhuj (the Vaiśeṣika), Akṣacaraṇa (the Nyāya), and Sugata (the Buddhist), which stand in opposition to the path of the Three Vedas (*trayīmārga*). This is expressed by the words "because of the impossibility of [their] arising" (*utpattyasaṃbhavāt*).
Thus, there is a lack of inclusion for those who know the Three Vedas, as well as for the acceptance of those outside the Three Vedas.
Even for the reasons just mentioned, that [case] is not the same as the recollections of Manu and others.

This being the case, there are also those who, while teaching many practices consisting primarily of minor arts such as incantations for deluding the world, causing hatred, expulsion, and subjugation, [preserve] only a few Vedic rites such as the worship of the Blessed One.
We consider those [teachings] propounded by the Pāñcarātrikas to be useless and untrustworthy, like milk placed in a dog-skin bag;
therefore, it is not logical that the Pañcarātra is rooted in the Veda.
It would attain authority, just like the treatises of Manu and others.
On this point, someone says: "Granted that the Vedas may be postulated as the cause for the Smṛtis of Manu and others, whose authority is separated by an intervening layer;
but what is the use of resorting to the Vedas as the basis for the Pañcarātra-smṛti?"

Even regarding the Vedas, that very experience which is the basis for their authority is indeed the cause of the remembrance of the Pañcarātra; for there is certainly no mutual relationship of source and derivative between the two remembrances of the Aṣṭakā and the rinsing of the mouth (ācamana), despite their having equal roots.
Two Smṛtis of equal status do not indeed depend upon each other;
likewise, the Pañcarātra and the Śruti do not depend upon one another.
The Pañcarātra falls into ruin by the loss of its basis in the Veda;
how could the Āgama not fall into ruin from the loss of that very basis?

He said: "In that case, are not even the Vedas of human origin, their authority being dependent upon human experience? Of what doubt could there be? For the nature of being a sentence is observed to consist in having its composition dependent on another."

If it is argued, "How else could this greatness of the knot called 'feeling' (vedanā) exist, such that even though it was not composed by anyone, it exists as a sentence?"— then, alas, this must indeed be the greatness of the smoke residing on the mountain!
Why should it not be possible that [the cognition] ascends to the expanse of the sky with an uninterrupted continuum even in the absence of such power?
But surely, how can there be a textual composition regarding a phenomenon that has transcended the scope of other means of valid cognition?

This is not so; for it is the Blessed One himself, who has directly realized dharma and adharma through innate intuition (*sahaja-saṃvedana*), who, out of compassion for the world, composed this book consisting of [the categories of] cognition and the rest.
Is there indeed any perception that has dharma and adharma as its object? Certainly.
Otherwise, how could he produce effects such as the body and the world? For he alone is the agent of something who is capable of directly perceiving its material cause and its instrumental causes;
and according to the Mīmāṃsakas as well, merit and demerit are the instrumental causes of the world.

This is indeed agreed upon. Therefore, some one who has directly realized that [reality] must be accepted as the one who fashioned the Vedas and so forth at the beginning; and as for the one who says that entities such as mountains and the world are not effects, one should reply to him as follows:
Entities that are the subject of dispute, such as the earth and so forth,
are effects because they possess a variegated structure, like a royal palace;
likewise, their destruction is also determined by the fact that they possess constituent parts.
And those entities which perish are destroyed by one who knows their means of destruction,
just as hailstones and the like are destroyed by us who know them.

Furthermore, those entities which are shattered by falling from trees or similar causes due to the intervention of an unseen intelligent agent are also subject to disagreement; thus, they do not bring about the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*).
Moreover, by means of the reason "possessing motion," which is supported by the quality of magnitude (*mahattva*):
In this context, it is appropriate to infer the arising and destruction of entities.

Thus, when the fact that the earth and other things are effects has been established by the logic set forth above, the Blessed One’s direct perception of the merit and demerit that serve as their instrumental causes is indeed proven. For it is said: "These entities under dispute, such as the earth, mountains, and so forth..."
These were created by some agent through the realization of what has been described.
Whatever possesses the nature of arising and perishing, and is thus characterized by origination and destruction,
is seen to be constructed by a similar agent, just as a house is.

Nor should it be argued that the creation of bodies, worlds, and so forth is an indispensable intermediate step for actions themselves while they are bringing about the desired ends of the person performing them; for,
unguided by a conscious agent, those actions are not capable of producing effects.
Or, because it is insentient, like an axe; for an axe, not presided over by a conscious carpenter, is not itself capable of producing sacrificial posts and the like.
Nor are we capable of creating things by presiding over *apūrvas*.
For we are not able to realize [it] directly prior to the arising of karma.
For it has been stated that agency resides only in one who directly perceives the materials and instruments [of action] in each respective case;
and no individual soul (kṣetrajña) is capable of directly perceiving the *apūrva* produced by karma.
Since it is perceived or asserted [as such],

one must therefore accept a certain Puruṣa of unsurpassed and diverse powers, who is capable of surveying the entire world— including the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), its enjoyments, the means thereof, and dharma and adharma. Of him...
Furthermore, non-obstructed knowledge and other such qualities are innate;
as it has been said:
"The knowledge of that Lord of the World is unobstructed, as is his dispassion."
Sovereignty and righteousness—this fourfold set is co-emergent with [the self].
Thus, the declarations of the mantras, arthavādas, itihāsas, and purāṇas corroborate this very point,
such as: "The one God, generating heaven and earth," and "Prajāpati created the Vedas," and so forth.

And at the beginning of time, during the period of dissolution (*pralayakāla*), that Blessed One exists with all instruments, bodies, and other means of enjoyment dissolved within his consciousness; for just as insentient things [are dissolved], so too are sentient beings devoid of instruments and bodies.
Because they did not become partakers of enjoyment, they are called "those who act as if insentient.
Having generated the entire world out of the great grace born from beholding the multitude of living beings who were thus acting [as if insentient],...

Having fashioned on one hand the triple Veda— which reveals the manifold means for attaining all the worldly prosperities desired by them— and then, with a mind inflamed by supreme compassion, repeatedly observing those submerged in the ocean of existence filled with various successions of misfortunes and remaining undisturbed despite their distress;

How could these tantras— which have as their root an independent experience equal to that of the three Vedas (trayī), and which were spoken by [the Lord] to Sanatkumāra, Nārada, and others, serving as the means for awakening to His own worship, which is the means for attaining the supreme ultimate good— be anything other than authoritative?
They preside over such various assemblies for the recollection of Manu and others.
This might indeed be so if the author of the Vedas were perceived through some means of valid cognition; however, he is not so perceived.
Nor can an author of the Veda be inferred by the mark of its being a sentence,
because there is the consequence that the intended specific meanings would be reversed;
for a sentence is observed to have a composition dependent upon another [an author].
All that which is spoken is perceived as belonging to one who possesses a body;
and for all embodied beings, the body exists by reason of merit and demerit.
Thus, for an embodied being who is not independent and whose pleasure and pain depend upon merit and its opposite,
the fact of his creation would lead one to infer that he is not the Lord.

Moreover, in this way, the status of being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatva*) is difficult to attain even for the Vedas; for it is impossible for them to have such validity regarding *dharma*, which is not previously known through other means of knowledge.

Now, one might ask: how can *dharma* be something not previously known through other means of knowledge? For it has been stated that [the Creator] directly perceives *dharma* and *adharma*; otherwise, how could he produce the world, which is the instrument for those two?
This is true as far as it goes, but there is no creator at all who fashions this entire universe.
There exists some creator by whom even this is thus imagined.
As for that which has been established by the reasoning of their variegated arrangement, it is replied: entities are perceived by worldly people in three ways.
Some of these, such as jars and the like, have makers perceived by direct observation;
others, such as the sky and so forth, are produced without [a perceptible] maker.
Some things, such as the earth and so forth, whose specific nature is subject to doubt, fall within those two categories previously shown;
in that case, there is no room for the operation of a creator deity. For the earth and so forth have existed in this very manner from time immemorial.
Regarding the gradual accumulation and depletion of adventitious factors, which do not undergo simultaneous arising and dissolution:
since such modes of origination and destruction are accepted even by the Mīmāṃsakas, this would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*).
Even that agency of an intelligent creator which has been established with such effort is already proven; for those who are intelligent are indeed sentient beings.
Through sacrifices and other rites, they produce various things for our own enjoyment.
And it is logical to postulate a presiding deity for those things established by both parties,
since we ourselves are capable of directly performing sacrifices, giving gifts, and so forth.
Let there be no perceptibility for that which is the potency-form of action and the referent of terms such as *apūrva*; for what use have we for it being perceived?

Indeed, potters and others, when about to undertake the production of effects such as jars, do not begin those respective works after having directly perceived the capacity of their materials and instruments— such as clay, the staff, and the wheel— to produce those specific effects.

If, for those who do not know the supreme power, the practical activity of undertaking means and so forth for the sake of achieving a desired end were untenable, it would be so; however, in this case, through the cognition born of the eternal scripture, they possess the proficiency to produce various [results] such as sacrifices, which have been fully ascertained.
By means of those very [elements], such as the earth and so forth, men manifest various states of being;
and thus it is said:
"One whose nature and instruments are directly perceived, who is skilled in the performance of actions..."
Nor is there any fixed rule that no one else is capable [of this].
Not seeing at all, this person remains in his own mind during the process of manifestation;
for how indeed could the Puruṣa be an agent with respect to knowledge?
Furthermore, the argument that "this entire universe is perishable because it is composed of parts" is invalid,
as its face is struck down by the superior force of direct perception.
"This is that very Meru, this is that orb of the sun,
and this is that very earth"— since such a clear cognition arises here [in the case of one who has attained samādhi].
For recognition itself is capable of making known their connection with all times; for there exist such persons who appear even in earlier and later times.

For those who possess such conditions and whose application [of the reason] is as follows: "A person is past time because he is time, just like the present time," [this is an instance of the fallacy of] recognition, such as that of the mountain, the rock, or the moth.
In this way, the application [of the argument] should also be shown regarding the future.
Nor does such an application entail the permanence of even a jar and the like,
because in that case, both destruction and arising are perceptible.
If, when there is contradiction, the self is not apprehended by some cause, then it follows that the self is not apprehended even in the absence of contradiction; thus, its existence is impossible.
Furthermore, the origination and destruction of the world which were established through the reasoning that it possesses motion while existing in a state of magnitude—
that too has its cause destroyed by the power of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
It would attain attractiveness today through this reasoning.

Furthermore, this reason—"because it is an effect"—is contradictory to the specific nature of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣaviruddha*). For "being an effect" is invariably concomitant with numerous specific qualities, such as having a visible body, not having one's desires fulfilled, lacking sovereignty, and lacking omniscience. These qualities are more intimately associated with the concept of being an effect than with the intended probandum.

How, indeed, could it [the inference] make known in the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin) those desired specific qualities—such as being bodiless, eternal, ever-satisfied, and omniscient—which are the very opposites of its own nature? Furthermore, even the act of impelling one's own body belongs only to one who possesses an effort whose non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) is a connection with a body, and not to anyone else. Thus, it is not so.
How could agency possibly belong to that which is bodiless?
Now, in order to avoid this fault, it is maintained that [the self] possesses a body; yet that body must either have a birth or not. If it has a birth, there would be an infinite regress.

If [the self] were eternal, it would also be a composite whole; thus, your argument is inconclusive. Furthermore, as for what they have said—that particularities are established by the force of the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*—this path also does not hold together.

For that reasoning would indeed survive even if there were a contradiction established by another means of knowledge; however, when no such [external] contradiction is observed, the contradiction [within the reasoning itself] becomes all the more evident.

Now, if even that which has ascertained the rule of invariable concomitance does not lead to the understanding that the earth and so forth have an intelligent cause, then the practical application of inference would be utterly extinguished; yet, if it does lead to such an understanding, [how can this be denied]?
This [inference] indeed makes known even that Creator who is expert in the construction of the entire triple world;

we do not say that it does not make him known, but rather that it presents all those specific features (viśeṣa) which were cognized at the time of grasping the pervasion (vyāpti), without distinction.

Nor does this lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), for when a probandum (liṅgin) falls within the scope of another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), the contrary particulars resulting from the force of the logical mark (liṅga) indeed obstruct that very [other] means of valid cognition; but here, what is sought to be established is the Blessed One, whose status as the object of another means of valid cognition has already been transcended.

It presents, without distinction, all those properties that possess an invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) as determined through positive and negative concomitance; and thus, there is an inconclusiveness (anaikāntya) with respect to things such as dūrvā grass sprouts growing near a courtyard, which arise from causes other than human activity.
Even in that case, the postulation of a super-sensory person as the presiding agent is mere imagination alone.
One should reflect upon this: in what place does he reside? Why is he eternally satisfied? And when does he produce all this in its entirety?
Sometimes, aiming for some desired result, every potter and the like produce something by means of their instruments; at other times, they produce whatever comes along.
If indeed play does not occur because [the Lord] has already accomplished his purpose,
then oh, the sovereign independence of the All-pervading Lord is now manifest!
Whatever he intends, he performs it without reflection,
being powerless in the great exertion involved in the birth, maintenance, and dissolution of the world.
If [it is argued that] living beings are created by one engaged in compassion, why are they not created happy? [This would be so] if it were dependent upon their own karma.
Consequently, there would be a loss of independence; moreover, since the diversity [of the world] is already established by those very same reasons, what is the use of this further hypothesis?
Therefore, there exists no such person who, being capable of creating the entire world,
has directly perceived dharma and adharma and composed the Vedas.
Furthermore, if the Vedas were created by someone, then their author would be that person by whom they were fashioned.
It would have to be remembered;
yet, just as it is not reasonable to remember [the builder of] a dilapidated well, so too it is not reasonable [to require the memory of an author] for the Veda,
because in that case there is no purpose for the author's remembrance.

Who indeed would have faith in those rituals— which consist of the relinquishing of many substances and are accomplished through immense exertion— without the recollection of an author who is highly trustworthy?
For instance, the Vedas are eternal, because they lack an author whose memory is not being recollected, even though such an author would be worthy of being remembered.

Those which do not possess the aforementioned probandum also do not possess the aforementioned means of proof, just like the *Mahābhārata* and other such works; however, these [Vedas] do possess the aforementioned means of proof, and therefore they necessarily possess the aforementioned probandum.
Consequently, the Vedas are not of human origin.
This has been stated by those whose intellects are deluded by their own dogmatic adherence:
"Just as the authority of the Veda is based upon direct experience, so too the authority of the Pañcarātra is based upon direct experience."

Now, what is this "authorlessness" (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Vedas? If it is the state of being composed of eternal phonemes (*varṇa``s`), this is equally true of the *Pañcarātra* tantras. If it is the eternity of the words (*pada``s`), that too is exactly the same. Nor is there eternity in the sequence (*anupūrvī`).
For a sequential order cannot constitute the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of eternal things.

If it is argued that the sequence of phonemes arises from the sequence of their utterance, then that sequence is indeed impermanent precisely because its cause is impermanent; what, then, is the distinction between the *Pañcarātra* and the Vedas?

This alone is the distinction: in one case, the independent person composes each respective sequence; in the other, the dependent person intends to express only that which has already been established by previous learners as a rule, along with the intermediate sub-classifications of order.
Since [the doctrine] established by the force of recognition cannot be denied, enough with this prolixity;
it is thus proven that the description of validity as being based on the experience of a distinct person is not the most excellent one.
Since no person who has directly perceived merit and demerit is established by means of valid cognition,
this tantra must have been composed by some man in order to delude the world.

Now, if it be argued that this [Lord] is sought to be established solely by the power of logic, let it be so; nevertheless, there is a refutation: for the Great Lord is indeed known through the authority of the Upanishads.

But when numerous eternal scriptural statements are indeed found that establish the Supreme Person— the omniscient Lord of all who is capable of creating the entire universe— how then can one refuse to accept the validity of the memory rooted in His direct experience?
Nor do those [scriptures] transgress the boundaries of valid cognition by having as their object established entities,
even though they are human words whose objects are far removed from the scope of other means of valid cognition.
Because it is impossible to prevent the validity [of a cognition] being established by its own inherent force (*svarasa*),

and because there is no possibility for either a proof or a refutation to apply to an already established entity (*siddha-vastu*), the word whose object is that [entity] is [invalidated] upon considering the reversal of the subsequent sublation (*bādhaka*) that was previously anticipated.

There would follow the loss of validity even for that which culminates in an action, because that [same consequence] applies there as well; for even an action such as the fetching of fuel-wood, being worldly, is indeed cognizable by other means of knowledge, since it is admitted that such an action can be known through another means of knowledge just like the cooking of rice.

Now, if the word that propounds an action (kārya) concerning the Agnihotra and other rites— which are distinct from [perceptible] characteristics— is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because no other means of knowledge could possibly apprehend it, then alas! [the same must apply to the Vedāntas].

In the Blessed One, whose body is a mass of unsurpassed awakening, sovereignty, and great bliss, there is not even a trace of connection with any other means of valid cognition; thus everything is the same, except for [our own] dogmatic attachment.
Moreover, even another means of valid cognition that has already functioned [regarding something else] does not [apply] to its own object by way of having that [Blessed One] as its object.

Since it does not fail to illuminate even that which is beyond [the senses], how could it be a mere restatement (anuvāda) on the grounds of the possibility of another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) occurring? Or rather, how could it be so for that which originates from the eternal scripture, which is untouched by any defects of human intentionality?

This is mere triviality: to claim that other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are sublated by the occurrence of various possible errors in a cognition that is being determined by its own prior sublation.

And thus, in the Blessed One, whose majesty consists of various forms of knowledge, sovereignty, and other powers attained through hundreds of scriptural revelations, defects such as being perceived as an ordinary being or having a limited physical form find no place, just as coldness and the like find no place in fire.
And therefore:
How can our tongue proceed to say that the Tantra, composed by the Omniscient One himself who is renowned at the summit of the Vedas, is false?
Oh, how great is the loss of effort for this dull-witted one! How can a mind once robust with the study of Mīmāṃsā now be so negligent?
Regarding an action not previously known through other means of knowledge, the wise, whose intellects are held in high esteem, consider the entirety of Vedic speech to be authoritative.
Because the derivation of words is determined by their being directed toward that [ultimate reality],
there is certainly no possibility of derivation when a word is directed toward something else.

For instance, when two elders are engaged in communication, one elder perceives an action residing in the other elder that arises immediately after hearing a word uttered by the first; and this perception leads to an inference based on the principle of "otherwise being inexplicable" (anyathānupapatti).
The power of a word is understood as terminating only in an action that brings about that [result],
for it is observed that within its own causal continuum, the cognition of the action itself serves as the cause for various specific activities;
thus, even here, seeing such an inclination, one concludes in this manner.
"Surely the cognition of this effect has arisen from his presence, since he proceeds immediately after this [cognition]"; and thus,
because it is intent upon establishing the effect as the cause for engagement that conforms to all worldly transactions.

When a word has been mastered, one determines that those portions of meaning which follow upon the insertion (āvāpa) and deletion (uddhāra) of words are denoted by their respective [words] because they are consistent with the primary action first apprehended; and in that context,
the optative suffixes (liṅ) and others are invariably associated with the cognition of that action.

The verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and so forth directly convey the very body of the action (*kāryaśarīra*), whereas the nominal suffixes (*kṛt*) and so forth experience that connection by means of presenting the adjuncts (*anubandha*) such as the person (*adhikāra*) required by it.

Nor can there be a determination of the power of a collection of words— terminating merely in the communication of the nature of events such as the birth of a son— to convey the desired birth of a son and so forth, based on [external signs] such as the emergence of horripilation and the expansion of the face.
Because it is impossible to determine that "this [cause] is this" when various causes for joy— whether unarisen, past, or present— are encountered;
by this, [it is shown that the same applies] even when there is a reference to the present occurring in conjunction with words that are either well-known or otherwise.
One must investigate the determination of the word-potency that is free from any other intended purpose (kārya). A person is taught there [in grammar] that "this word" has such-and-such a form,
and it is in accordance with that very form that other words are derived.
It has been established that these [words] convey their own meanings as connected with an action;
now, because they are the cause of the cognition thereof, their authority pertains to things already existing.
If it is maintained that this [reason] is inconclusive (*anekānta*) with respect to words, that is not tenable;
if, on the other hand, its being directed toward that [meaning] is the reason, then there would be the fallacy of the unestablished (*asiddhatā*).
For a verbal cognition never culminates with respect to an entity that does not have the nature of an effect.

As for those cognitions of concomitance (*anvaya*) that arise immediately after hearing worldly words, they are said to be inferential (*ānumānika*) and not verbal (*śābdī*); thus, [the distinction] is indeed logically established.
The ultimate purport of those [scriptural passages] is this:
if there were no apprehension of words as having that [injunction] as their primary purpose,
why would the injunction "One should offer the Agnihotra" be accepted?
Now, even though validity has been established there [in the Veda] by that much alone,
an injunction is nevertheless accepted for the sake of attaining human goals.
Therefore, the activity of the means of valid cognition does not follow from the requirements of a purpose;
rather, it is the adoption of a purpose that is rooted in those [means].
Indeed, it is not the case that because one desiring gold has no interest in looking at a stone, it is therefore appropriate to resort to looking at the gold;
for the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of words is not established until it reaches its final purpose.
In the case of an instruction regarding the present tense and so forth, one does not assume a prescriptive rule.

And thus, even the meaning of the Upaniṣads must be explained as being subordinate to injunctions for knowledge, meditation, and so forth, which are recorded here and there; therefore, this is the meaning: [one should know] the Self as omniscient and blissful.
One should understand [it] thus:

yet by that much, even the intrinsic nature (svarūpa) is not established; for it must be understood that such an injunction is possible even when that very form is non-existent, just as one might say, "one should recognize him as a father" even when he is not actually a father.

And likewise, there is the injunction for the *udgītha* regarding the syllable *oṃ*, even though it is not itself the *udgītha*. Furthermore, those passages which teach the reality and eternity of the Self imply the enjoyment of fruits in the hereafter, as they do not specify a particular time for the performance of the ritual action.

Therefore, since these [scriptural passages] are intent upon establishing a conscious creator, not even a single word among them is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding a factual reality. Consequently, this applies to all explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).

By establishing that [the passage] is intent upon demonstrating the weeping of Rudra and so forth as already accomplished, it has also been shown that its connection with injunctive words located at a great distance is merely commendatory;
therefore, for those who have not reflected upon the intended meaning of the preceding and following words, [this appears to be]—
Enough with this excessive detail; it has been established that this person, whose form is fashioned by faith, is merely "proclaimed.
Thus, it is proven that even from scripture, no excellence of the desired Person is established.
Furthermore, let it be granted that even an existing entity may be the subject matter of a treatise; nevertheless—

How indeed can it be accepted that anyone understands dharma and adharma while disregarding the cognition produced by Vedic injunction (codanā)? For omniscience is compatible even with one who understands objects according to their nature through well-known means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); for there is no such statement [to the contrary].
This makes known his omniscience by way of eliminating the causes for the arising of well-known [erroneous] cognitions;
even if something were to exist, it would still be so.
Since the meanings of the words are unfit for mutual connection, it must be supported as being merely an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*);
for the cognition of the sentence-meaning arising from the words is preceded by the apprehension of compatibility and other factors through other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
We consider how it could possibly come into existence when there is a contradiction with another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that has already fallen [upon the object] earlier and been awaited;
for if a statement has its scope rejected by perception and other such means of knowledge, how could it arise?
Who indeed could deny the identity between the sun and the sacrificial post?
Furthermore, even if there were some person who was the locus of such extraordinary qualities,
what would that have to do with the validity of the treatise one wishes to establish?

But surely those who follow the *Pañcarātra* tradition remember that this was composed by such a person; why do the *Pāśupatas* not likewise remember it? For they too declare their own system's founder to be the sovereign lord of the entire universe.
The same applies to others as well.

Nor are all of these omniscient, because it is impossible for them to teach contradictory doctrines. Furthermore, whatever reason one might employ to establish the omniscience of a single proponent...

Since this [teaching] is common to all, when many people here are teaching mutually contradictory meanings in a competitive spirit of "I first, I first," which one among them can we determine to be omniscient?
As it has been said:
"When there are many omniscient beings who teach contradictory doctrines,
and all possess equal grounds for their claims, who indeed can be identified as the one [true one]?"
Thus,
the postulation of an omniscient being depends upon an independent realization; however,
due to their mutual contradiction, this would result in the invalidity of all [such claims].
But surely, how can this [work] be placed on the same level as other tantras when it was spoken by Vāsudeva, who is renowned in the Śruti and Smṛti?
For thus the majesty of that [Puruṣa] is heard in the Pauruṣa Sūkta:
"From his feet came the earth, from his ears the directions, and likewise from his eyes the sun and so forth, as well as what is beyond."
"Dhātṛ fashioned the sun and the moon as they were before";
likewise, "He is Brahmā, He is Śiva," and "That is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu; there is no lord over Him in the world."
"He has no ruler, nor indeed any mark"—
thus the Śrutis proclaim His glory,
characterized by the creation, sustenance, and dissolution of the universe.
"The universe has arisen from Viṣṇu and remains within him alone;
he is the author of its maintenance and withdrawal," so said Parāśara.
Thus Manu also spoke of that very Lord of All, as follows:
"Nārāyaṇa is beyond the unmanifest; from the unmanifest arises the Egg.
Thus, he is continuously praised by the various words of the Śrutis and the sages.
The Supreme Person, possessing knowledge and sovereignty, composed the Pañcarātra;
if that were to be equated with those systems that have strayed from the path of the Vedas on the grounds of being "protectors," then the drinker of Soma would be classed as a drinker of wine.

This is not superior; for what reason, my dear, would the attributes of pure knowledge, sovereignty, and so forth not be well-known in the Śrutis regarding the Blessed Lord, the Conqueror of Tripura? Therefore, this [objection] is trivial. Or rather, that very God is the cause of both the preservation and the destruction of the abode of the three worlds.
How can he who takes the Vedānta as his sole authority speak of one who stands outside the assembly of those learned in the Vedas?
For indeed, many Vedic scriptures are found that declare the omniscience and omnipotence even of the Blessed Lord Paśupati:
"He who is all-knowing, he who is all-perceiving; Him, the supreme Maheśvara among lords."

And so forth. Furthermore, the two words "omniscient" (*sarvajña*) and "Lord" (*īśvara*), even though they may apply elsewhere, do not apply to anyone other than the God who wields the Pināka bow (Śiva), because of their inherent power of origin.
Furthermore, once the omniscient one has been established by the word "sarvajña," the inclusion of the term "sarvavit" would result in redundancy for you.
Therefore, this term "omniscient" has Mahādeva as its sole referent;
likewise, the Skanda, Liṅga, and other Purāṇas [affirm] the wielder of the Pināka bow.
They have been exhausted in the production of omniscience and universal sovereignty;
therefore, by this reasoning, its authority follows from the fact that it was composed by Him.
Since the Pāśupata Tantra has been obtained, there arises the consequence that the validity of all Tantras is subverted due to their mutual contradictions.

Moreover, let it be granted that the Blessed One Vāsudeva is indeed the Puruṣa of the Upaniṣads; yet, how could he possibly be imagined to have composed this system which stands in opposition to the Vedas, when he himself declared, "The Śruti and Smṛti are my very commands"? And therefore:
We conclude that this tantra, which has been composed and presented under the name of Vāsudeva, was produced by someone seeking to deceive.
Or let it be that Vāsudeva himself, the sovereign of the entire world, is the author of this system;
nevertheless, by Hari, through a form intended to delude Māyā, [there was] the destruction of the host of those who hate the gods.
For they say that those [words] spoken under the guise of deluding [the enemy] are intended to destroy his enemies.
Thus, as he was entering and exiting the vast cavern of his own great illusory power (māyā), what did he say? When the doubt arose as to whether this was so or not, how was the resolution reached?
On the contrary, it is understood that he spoke while actually causing confusion,
because the Vedic [tradition] does not accept it, just as is the case with the doctrine of the Arhatas.

Furthermore, the fact that the Veda does not accept [the Pañcarātra] has already been explained in detail; therefore, it is not a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) by virtue of being rooted in independent experience,
nor is it like the tradition of Manu and others— thus, the tradition of the Pañcarātra is untenable.
If the Lord, having obtained the meaning of the Vedas from a teacher who was satisfied by his service— just like Manu and others— composed this Tantra;
If that were the case, the postulation of his independence would be useless and false;
for it would be extraordinary to claim that the Veda appears to him even without having been studied.
In this regard, all those defects raised by the author of the Vārttika—
such as the [necessity of] a superior person (puruṣātiśaya) and so forth— should be carefully considered.
Furthermore,
according to the Smṛti, heresy consists of the Śaiva, Pāśupata, Buddhist, Ārhata, Kāpāla, and Pañcarātra systems.
Furthermore, by the act of classifying it as "Vaidika" and "Tāntrika," the certainty that the Pañcarātra is outside the Veda (vedabāhya) is understood.
"The Śaiva, Pāśupata, Saumya, and Lāguḍa—these fourfold divisions of Tantra have been declared; one should not practice them in a confused manner. Thus it is said. Likewise:
"The Bhākta, the Bhāgavata, and the Sātvata—these are considered the threefold [division].
Such a statement regarding the classification of tantras is also seen in the Pañcarātra.
Furthermore:
To claim that a statement devoid of logic— one concerning the birth of the individual soul (*jīva*) and other matters rejected by *Śruti* and *Smṛti*— is true is a great laugh.

And thus says the Śruti: "Verily, O Maitreyī, this Self is indestructible and of an imperishable nature; its association with the elements (mātrās) occurs [only through limiting adjuncts]. Likewise: "Indeed, it is when deprived of the living self (jīva) that this body dies; the living self does not die."
It might be argued that this statement merely establishes the absence of annihilation and does not convey the absence of birth.
This is not so; for by the mention of non-annihilation, the absence of birth is determined.
For it is impossible that an entity which has been born should not perish.

But surely, because of the determination of the oneness of Being in the passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," it is concluded that prior to the time of creation, individual souls did not exist;
for if the souls were separate prior to creation, they would have to be like the Supreme Self.

How is it that this determination of oneness—“Being alone [existed]”—is made? To this it is replied: That determination of oneness expressed as “Being alone” has as its scope the wind, water, space, and so forth, which were intended to be created.
If this statement had intended to exclude [the possibility],
then its production would have been pointed out as being like that of the sky-flower and so forth.
And because it is not so specified, the living being (jīva) does not undergo birth;
for in such passages as "It created fire," the creation of the living being is indeed heard by us [in scripture].
But is it not the case that in the passage "from which indeed these beings [arise]," it is the living beings themselves whose birth, life, departure, and dissolution are perceived?
For this term "beings" (bhūta) is a designation for living beings.
Because it is seen in such passages as, "Causing all beings to whirl," and so forth.
For this word "living" (jīvanti) is applicable only to those who are alive;
therefore, it is understood that the statement "they are born" refers to living beings.
This is untenable; for the word *bhūta* is well-established as referring to space, wind, fire, water, and earth.
This term [the self] applies to those [elements] only through the function of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
And life is said to undergo many kinds of transformation.
Those [elements] such as earth and so forth, which were first understood through the word *bhūta*, express their meaning by virtue of being concordant with that; thus the words "live" (*jīvanti*).
And if the word *bhūta* applies to a living being (*jīva*), then—
He also says that his birth is bound to the body.
Therefore, even though the word *bhūta* refers to the individual soul (*jīva*),
the use of the word "are born" (*jāyante*) is appropriate, just as one says, "the ox is born and goes."
Likewise, we possess other scriptural passages such as "For the soul is one," as well as the words of the Blessed One which declare that the individual souls are unproduced.
"Know that both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are indeed beginningless;
unborn, eternal, constant, and ancient is this [Self]; it is never born, nor does it ever die," and so forth.
And this is the logical reasoning as well.
The living being under dispute never undergoes birth,
because it possesses substantiality while being formless and having consciousness as its nature, like the supreme Self.
Observing the refutations against its being of human origin along the stated lines,
some, finding no other recourse, established the Tantra as eternal.
This [argument] is stated while being obstructed by the failure to remember the agent who is more clearly established within one's own heart; therefore, it should be disregarded.
Furthermore:
In this way, why would the logic of the Pāśupatas and others not be restrained by the staff?
If one were to say, "Let it be so," there would be mutual contradiction.
And the fact that [the Mahābhārata] was composed by Vāsudeva is renowned throughout the entire world;
it cannot be set aside, just as the non-human authorship of the Veda cannot be denied.

Furthermore, if someone were to say: "When validity possesses three characteristics whose objects are free from non-arising and error, which one of these is being extolled here?", he should be told: "O Lāguḍamati, do you not know that it is precisely that which you desire? Having understood this, let your mind be stilled."
Thus, by propounding doctrines that contradict the logic, Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇas as they have been set forth, and by being devoid of acceptance by all cultured people (śiṣṭas),
some person has sought to deceive the world under the pretext of teaching [the means to] heaven and liberation.
We consider that the *Pañcarātra* tantras were composed [by humans].
Such a statement falls precisely within the scope of forgetfulness.
"Those *smṛtis* which are outside the Veda, and whatever false views there may be... [and so forth].
All those are fruitless after death; for they are remembered as having darkness as their ultimate end.
Thus,
even those who follow such evil paths have their worship prohibited by these [teachings], even in mere words; and it has been said:
And these very ones are those for whom there is not even worship with mere words:
the heretics, those established in improper actions, those who act like cats, and the rogues.
"One should not honor even with mere words those who rely on logic (*haituka*) and those who act like herons (*bakavṛtti*).
According to the principle thus presented, [one should reject] the Pañcarātra in its entirety.
It follows that [the cognition] would be invalid; this being the case, it is stated in reply:
Let it be accepted that the Tantra under dispute is authoritative,
because it arises from faultless knowledge, like the injunctions for the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices.
In this inference, the faults scrutinized in the Nyāya-śāstra cannot yet be sought; therefore, let the subject (pakṣa) be examined there.
A "thesis" (pakṣa) is the meaning of the proposition; it is that which, being qualified by something already established, is desired by oneself to be proven as something not yet established.

In this regard, the thesis is not one whose qualifier is unestablished, because the category of reality known as "validity" is established for both disputants with respect to perception and the other means of knowledge;
nor is it one whose qualificand is unestablished, because the *Pañcarātra* scripture is well-known to all the world.

Nor is it a case of proving what is already established, because the validity of the treatise under discussion is not admitted by the opponent; nor is it contradicted by perception, because invalidity is beyond the reach of the senses; nor is it contradicted by inference, because there is no such apprehension [of a contradictory reason].

But surely inference is indeed perceived: "The Pañcarātra scripture is not authoritative because it is outside the Veda, like the Buddhist Āgama. To this we reply: what kind of non-authoritativeness is intended to be established here? If—

Consequently, the characteristic of the non-arising of knowledge would entail a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), for direct perception indeed arises immediately upon hearing the words of the *Pañcarātra* scripture for a listener who has already understood the relationship between the words and their meanings.
Knowledge has that object as its domain.

Nor does it possess the characteristic of doubt, for the same reason of contradiction; for indeed, the statement "one should worship the Supreme Person, the four-armed one, in the midst of the lotus" does not mean "should one worship him or not?"
It produces a cognition that is characterized by doubt, nor does it possess the characteristic of error,

because there is an absence of a non-perception of the fit [object]; for the postulation of a future error would contradict direct perception and would result in the destruction of all worldly activity, as will be explained in detail.
This will be explained further below.
Moreover, it contradicts scripture (*āgama*),
because in the *Pañcarātra-āgama* it is understood that one's own purpose (*svārtha*) is exactly like that.
Now, if that [scripture] lacks authoritative status, its contradiction [of another position] is not a valid objection.

Alas! This being the case, there is a circular argument (*anyonyāśrayaṇa*): if that [Veda] lacks authority, then inference has authority; and if inference has authority, then that [Veda] lacks authority.
Furthermore, what is this "being outside the Veda" (*vedabāhyatva*)? If it means simply "being other than the Veda," then...

[The reason is] inconclusive with respect to perception and so forth. If the reason is then qualified by adding "provided it possesses the nature of being a word" (*śabdatve sati*), that constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). As they say: "Furthermore, the introduction of a qualification when a reason was stated without one is a point of defeat. Moreover, [the reason remains] inconclusive with respect to the statements of Manu and others.
Now, O dull-witted logician, to eliminate this fault, do you perhaps think that because [the system] is called "outside the Veda" (*vedabāhya*), it must lack a basis in the Veda? What is this?

Therefore, the meaning [of the reason] is: "because, while being a word (*śabdatve sati*), it is not rooted in the Veda. Consequently, there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) due to the Vedas. Alternatively, the reason is: "because, while not being the Veda (*avedatve sati*) and while being a word (*śabdatve sati*), it is not rooted in the Veda. Even so, there are [counter-examples], such as the authoritative instruction: "There are trees on the bank of the river."
If it is not rooted in the Vedas, the fallacy of inconclusiveness (anaikāntya) unavoidably follows.

Now, if the reason (*hetu*) is defined as "being non-Vedic while being verbal, while having an object that is a product, and while not being rooted in the Veda," even here there is a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as "one should eat slowly when one has indigestion.
Furthermore, even if it is qualified by the aforementioned attributes and has dharma and adharma as its object—
The reason "because it is rooted in the Veda" is one that is partially unestablished (*bhāgāsiddha*), for the Pañcarātra scripture does not cover the entire domain of dharma and adharma;
rather, it consists predominantly of statements concerning Brahman alone.
If the qualification "provided that the object is not amenable to other means of valid cognition" is added,

even then the same [fallacy of] unestablishedness remains, because it is well known from hundreds of scriptural passages that the Blessed One’s direct perception has as its domain all things, including dharma, adharma, and so forth.
We shall explain this very point immediately hereafter; therefore, enough of this display of unstable eloquence by those who have not studied the system of Akṣapāda.
Even other possible inferences will be set forth and refuted later on; therefore, the thesis is not contradicted by inference,
nor is it contradicted by scripture.
Because hundreds of scriptures, such as the one beginning with "This is the Great Upaniṣad," which establish the authority of the *Pañcarātra* treatise, will be demonstrated;
[and because of] one's own words and one's own admissions—

The types of contradiction with verbal expression that conflict with what is well-known to the entire world are indeed not to be suspected here; for instance, there is first of all no contradiction with one's own statement (*svavacanavirodha*). That [contradiction] is threefold: contradiction with the mere utterance, contradiction with the utterance of a property (*dharma*), and contradiction with the utterance of a substratum (*dharmin*). Among these, it is not [the case that there is a contradiction with the mere utterance].

To that extent, this thesis is contradicted merely by its own statement; for the declarative proposition "the Pañcarātra scripture is authoritative" does not subvert its own meaning, unlike [the statement] "I shall remain silent for as long as I live. Nor is there a contradiction with the teaching of Dharma, for [the scripture's] authority is not...
It refutes the position being prescribed under the heading of the *Pañcarātra*,

just as the statement that all sentences are false [refutes its own basis]; nor is there a contradiction with the statement regarding the locus (*dharmī*), because even when the locus exists, the connection of the property (*dharma*) is not contradictory, just as [the property of] being a mother [is not contradictory to the existence of the woman].
The status of being a *pañcarātra* scripture is incompatible with its validity as a barren [non-authoritative] entity;
for when one asserts the validity of that which is the subject of dispute, there is no contradiction with the specific property of the subject as stated in the Veda.

Since there is no dispute regarding the fact that even those for whom non-violence is prescribed are subject to the characterization of unrighteousness, there is consequently no contradiction with scripture; thus is the thesis established.

Nor are there defects such as the inconclusiveness of the reason (*hetu*). To explain: it is not first of all inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), for that is of two kinds, distinguished as common (*sādhāraṇa*) and uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*);
for example, in the proof of the permanence of earth, "knowability" (*prameyatva*) is the common [inconclusive] reason.
In that case, the possession of odor belongs exclusively to [earth] alone;

therefore, the state of being a cause of faultless cognition is not common to both valid and invalid cognitions, such that it would be a "common inconclusive" (sādhāraṇānaikāntika) reason. For indeed—
The state of being a cause of faultless knowledge has already been observed in counter-examples such as the deceptive speech of those who are not authoritative;
nor is it an "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) reason, precisely because the example of sentences concerning the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and others has been stated.
The positive concomitance with the similar class (*sapakṣānvaya*) has been demonstrated.
Nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*), because there is no contrary pervasion (*viparītavyāpti*); for the state of being the cause of faultless cognition is not pervaded by invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*).
Nor is it "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), because there is no contradiction with direct perception and because it is in accordance with scripture.
Nor is it "unestablished" (*asiddha*); for unestablishment occurs either by way of the locus (*āśraya*) or by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*).
First, there is no lack of a locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), because the *Pañcarātra* scripture serves as the locus;
nor is there a lack of the essential nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*), which is threefold due to the distinctions of ignorance, doubt, and error.
First, there is no lack of [the reason] through ignorance, because words establishing it have been uttered. Nor...
It is not "doubtful-unestablished" (saṃdigdhāsiddha), because the speaker himself has established the absence of defects,
and for the opponent as well, it is established without effort simply through the non-perception of any defects;
as for its being "unestablished by the contrary" (viparyayāsiddhi), that is cast far away indeed.
Now, how is the suspicion of defects that arises from the commonality of being of human origin removed in the case of the *Pañcarātra* mantras; or how is that same suspicion,
