which arises in the Vedas from the commonality of being sentences, warded off by [the claim of] their being of non-human origin?
Therefore, even in this case, having understood that [the teaching] was composed by the Supreme Person who has attained all knowledge and fulfilled all desires,
may you find peace.
This is what is meant:
Intrinsic defects that obstruct the validity of a word do not exist at all;
rather, its status as a means of valid cognition is intrinsic—this is the established position.
In certain cases, that [reliability] is set aside due to a defect in the speaker’s intention,
as in such statements as, "There is a herd of elephants on the tip of a finger," and so forth.
In this composition of the present work, the resonance of the Threefold Supreme (Trayīmūrdhan) alone wipes away from us any suspicion of fault that might arise regarding the intention of the speaker.
Indeed, the Vedāntas proclaim [the Lord] as the omniscient master of the universe and the supremely compassionate one; how, then, could there be deception and the like toward Him?
But is it not the case that I have stated that words do not possess authority regarding established entities,
because the acquisition of linguistic competency does not occur through the usage of others in those cases?
Thus, even when expressing a meaning that is not established [by other means],
ordinary people understand it through usage, just as they understand the capacity [of words] from such things as the fulfillment of a purpose.
For example, immediately after hearing the words "a son has been born to you," and immediately following the distinct expansion of the face produced thereby, one perceives,
"this person is joyful," and concludes that this joy is based on the comprehension of a pleasant object.

Observing within himself that even in a middle-aged or elderly person joy is based solely upon that [word], and being permeated by that state of being, he determines that it is the word itself which brings about the cognition of the beloved object.
Even there, when doubts arise as to who this speaker might be among the various causes of joy— past, future, and so forth— that are surging forth,
[the certainty arises] from the subsequent realization of his birth and deeds.
Previously, he was certain that there must be some other being who had become the cause of that.
"What is the reason for the conviction that 'the birth-rite must be performed'?
Reflecting thus, one understands that it is simply because what is well-known is dear."
A child desiring to learn [the meaning of words] understands that "the birth of a son" alone is what is being expressed;
and in that regard,
the determination of the power (śakti) of individual words occurs through the method of insertion and exclusion (āvāpoddhāra).
The expression "it is established" thus denotes both an accomplished and an unaccomplished object.
Now, it is not the case that the relationship of cause and effect is established merely by the fact that one thing occurs when another exists, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor is the understanding of the duty to perform the birth-rite necessarily preceded by the comprehension of a desired object, for it is observed [otherwise].

Even for one whose mind is distressed by the toil of maintaining a family, the comprehension of what ought to be done— even if preceded by a lack of pleasure— is observed; is this comprehension of duty ever seen to be caused by words,
such that in commands like "Bring the cow," there arises the comprehension of the duty to bring the cow?
It is accepted that [the cognition] has sound as its cause.
If it is argued that, since a spontaneous origin is untenable, the sound present at that very moment is the cause for its apprehension, this same principle applies elsewhere as well.

Furthermore, even that capacity to convey an object which serves as a cause for activity— wherever it occurs— is understood to be devoid of a cause [other than the word] when it is expressed by verbal suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*).
Furthermore, even for one who maintains that all words have only functional significance (*kāryaparatā*),

it must be established that words such as "cow" or "horse" denote those things whose individual forms are determined through the methods of inclusion (*āvāpa*) and exclusion (*uddhāra*); and even when so established, [the denotation remains restricted].
If it is argued that [the word] is capable only when connected with its effect (kārya), then enough of this obsession;
for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is possible even through the denotation of what is connected with something else.
This capacity to denote a meaning already connected [with another] must necessarily be accepted.
For otherwise, it would be difficult to maintain that words denote things as connected with an action.
Furthermore, this [position] is underinclusive,

because it is subject to the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and the like; for optative suffixes and so forth denote their own meaning as being connected precisely with the adjuncts (*anubandha*) such as the qualification (*adhikāra*) and others that are already established.

If it is argued that "in those [words] there is the denotation of the related" (*anvitābhidhāna*), while "in the other [the verb] there is the denotation of what is related to an action" (*kāryānvitābhidhāna*), that would be like the "half-old woman" fallacy (*arddhajaratīya*); therefore, it is better to adopt the theory of the denotation of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*) everywhere.
Thus: "Because of the connection with another word that is required, proximate, and capable..."
All proponents of philosophical systems must accept that words derive their meaning from their own primary referents.
Although the power of a word is indeed to be understood only through the comprehension of the impossibility of [otherwise] initiating activity, nevertheless,
for the sake of ascertaining that power of the word,
it is proper to rely upon the effect merely as an external means, like the space in which the speaker stands.
Those learned in the principles of logic maintain that the meaning of a word cannot be obtained through any other means;
therefore, there can be no syntactic connection (*samanvaya*) with an action (*kārya*) that serves merely as a means.
In the case of those proficient in worldly transactions, it is just as with crossing on water and so forth;

for indeed, even though [the knowledge of] crossing on water and the like is useful for determining specific gems such as diamonds belonging to the class of "Brahma" (or similar categories), once the existence of the gem has been determined, [that utility no longer applies].
There is utility [of the word] in the state of linguistic usage; likewise,
even for an effect that was useful at the time of acquiring proficiency, there is no utility in the state of having already attained proficiency.

If words convey only an object as connected with an action, how can there be from them an understanding of a relation such as a river being crossed or a fruit being attained, which is already established? If it is argued that this [understanding] is not primary (mukhya) but figurative (lākṣaṇika), then where indeed is the primary usage of words?
If it is argued that [the word] denotes an effect not previously known through other means of knowledge (*mānāntarāpūrva*), we say no;
for since there can be no linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) regarding such an entity, its usage would be untenable.
Indeed, a linguistic convention with respect to something not previously known through other means of knowledge is not possible.
Nor can there be a cognition from words whose meanings are not understood, because that would lead to over-extension.

Furthermore, there is one who thinks: "In the world, a person proficient in linguistic usage rejoices in the Veda, which—by the force of its co-occurrence with the word for the result (*phala*)—possesses the power to denote a novel causal entity (*apūrva-kārya*) that transcends the meanings of verbal roots such as sacrifice, the transitory nature of which is understood through that very co-occurrence; however, in the world..."
Even for one who is deluded, since worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is possible, he does not care to ascertain the true nature of the meaning of words.
This [assertion] of his is merely a wishful thought; for [it is not the case that] in the performance of an action...
It establishes that the effect resides in the already proficient [learner], for otherwise there would be an over-extension [of the argument].
If the comprehension of the syntactic relation were not possible while adhering to the word-potency as it has been mastered in the linguistic usage of elders, [then the following would occur].

It does not arise that, because of its impossibility, one should abandon the established power [of the word] and resort to another power of the word; rather, let figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) be resorted to as desired. For when there is the co-occurrence of words with contradictory meanings—
The denotation of words is itself interpreted otherwise,

because otherwise there would follow the consequence of a lack of confidence in all word-meanings. Furthermore, [words] possess the capacity to convey an action not previously known through other means of knowledge.
It is not accepted, for the time being, for the sake of establishing a connection between action and its fruit.

The relationship belongs to that which is produced by an injunction (*naiyogika*), and not again to that which is inherent in the nature of things (*vainiyogika*); it consists of an effect that transcends the meaning of the verbal root, and does not arise from the connection between an action and its fruit.
Without it, the relationship is not established; and without that [relationship], it certainly does not exist.
Consequently, there is a circularity (*itaretarāśraya*) that is difficult to resolve.
[For] it is the motivator of a person who is already distinguished by the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), namely heaven.
If it were not so, then the injunction would not be a means for accomplishing the intended purpose.
Furthermore, the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*), being transitory, cannot be conceived as the instrument (*karaṇa*);
thus, it is said that [the suffix] conveys an object that is a distinct result from that [root-meaning].
For this [act] is not qualified by the goal to be accomplished, namely heaven;
rather, it is the person desiring heaven who is enjoined here.
For heaven cannot be a qualification of the person entitled [to the rite], because it is that which is to be accomplished;
indeed, only that which is already established can be a qualification for every person to be enjoined (*niyojya*).
Just as living and so forth are qualifications here, so too is desire alone the qualification.
Furthermore, what kind of "status as an end to be accomplished" (sādhyatva) belongs to heaven and the like when they are experienced merely as qualifiers of the person to be enjoined?
If it is said to be the fitness for connection with a means, that alone is not sufficient.
Heaven must be attained as long as there is no birth through yoga.

The fact that [the Veda] culminates in its accomplishment is based solely on the mandate (niyoga) as its means of valid cognition; yet if the mandate is established by that [accomplishment] and that [accomplishment] is established by the mandate, there is certainly a circular argument.
If heaven were the goal to be accomplished and not the mandate (niyoga),
then two goals cannot coherently maintain a relationship within a single sentence.

For two independent things to be established as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) is not consistent; however, these two things to be established (*sādhya*) are consistent, because the attainment of heaven is inseparable from the fulfillment of the injunction (*niyoga*). As it has been said regarding the fulfillment of the injunction:

If it is argued that "everything is consistent with that [the injunction]," and that "the accomplishment of the fruit is for the sake of accomplishing the injunction," and therefore there is no contradiction— this is not so. For what indeed is not accomplished by the injunction without the accomplishment of heaven?
There is no qualification, no object, nor anything else required by an injunction.
For in the case of obligatory duties (nitya-adhikāra), the injunction does not depend upon that [desire];
nor is it the case that an injunction toward one thing is untenable for one who desires something else.
The majesty of *niyoga* alone is such that it is enjoined even upon eternal things;
for *niyoga*, being understood as the primary factor, draws toward itself even one who desires heaven.
Just as it impels one even against one's will toward obligatory rites that bear no fruit.
Furthermore:
For one who desires heaven indeed blinks and even opens his eyes;
yet those sacrifices are not for the sake of accomplishing heaven—why is this not accepted?
If it is argued that many things are apprehended as being the means to that [result],
then are sacrifices and the like also apprehended by that cognition while being excluded from the injunction?
And in that regard:
"As long as there are no injunctions intent upon establishing the relationship between the goal to be accomplished and the means of accomplishment, all ritual acts remain fruitless."

Therefore, it is logical that first there is the comprehension of being a means to a desired end from the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth, and subsequently, activity arises from passion (*rāga*); thus, it is untenable to claim that the primary denotative power (*mukhyā śaktiḥ*) belongs only to the apūrva as the object to be accomplished (*kārya*), while in other cases it is merely figurative (*lākṣaṇikī*). For this very reason, according to the respective circumstances—
From worldly words, cognitions arise whose objects are things established by those [words]. But are these not born from the power of the word? Indeed, they are inferential;
for even words that possess the capacity to convey meanings known at the time of linguistic convention do, in some cases, [function as such].
Obstructed by doubts produced by the observation of deviation, the mere hearing [of words] does not determine their meaning; nor does an undetermined meaning become known,
because there is no such thing as a cognition whose nature is uncertainty.
Even when the meaning of the sentence is not yet known, the hearer reflects thus:
"This person is uttering words whose meanings are mutually related and capable of being connected."
Furthermore, trustworthy persons do not employ words whose relationships [to their meanings] are unknown;
therefore, one understands that such a person possesses knowledge of the positive concomitance (anvaya).

Thus, when the inferential knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) has been inferred, the object demonstrated by it does not require a verbal expression; therefore, since worldly speech is dependent upon the speaker's experience, its function culminates in that very [experience].

That is incorrect; for a word that makes an object known by its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be expected to abandon its natural capacity to convey meaning simply because it is found to be false in some instance due to being influenced by defects in the speaker's intention, since the possibility of such [defects] exists elsewhere as well. Indeed, not...

In the state of being neutralized by mantra (*mantrapratihata*)— where the reading *mantrapratihatidaśāyām* is appropriate, or alternatively, it should be understood that the suffix *kta* in the word *hata* denotes the abstract state (*bhāve*)— the fire does not burn; likewise, elsewhere too, one does not burn due to the apprehension of such a state, nor does one [burn].

Just as the sense organ, having perceived the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell— which deviates from the actual object— does not cause one to understand a jar or other objects due to the influence of defects, so too, for a listener who has already mastered the connection between words and their meanings, the word causes the meaning to be understood instantaneously without waiting for a primary (underlying) cognition.
Even when an object is presented prior to the full comprehension of the fundamental knowledge, how could an inference such as "how does this person know it thus? proceed?
Do you desire to infer that "this speaker knows something" because you wish to infer a cognition of the connection with a qualified object?
It cannot be said that the speaker did not know anything at all;
for both speech and linguistic usage may have as their object the meaning of a sentence.

Inference, which has as its object the connection with a qualified meaning, is impossible without a prior mental cognition directed toward that object; therefore, the meaning of the word must be understood beforehand, for [inferences] do not occur without having attained a connection with a specific object.
Cognitions differ from one another;
however, a specific object is not established by means of such inferred cognitions in the same way that a sentence structure is capable of conveying a corresponding syntactic connection (*anvaya*).

If it is argued that it brings about the knowledge of the positive concomitance (anvaya) of those [reasons], then the concomitance of the objects must have already been understood; for a concomitance that has not been projected (*āropita*) into the cognition cannot delimit the formal application (*prayoga*).
Therefore, in cases such as "there is fruit on the riverbank," that cognition which has an established object is verbal, not inferential.
Consequently, the word is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only with respect to an unprecedented effect (*apūrvakārya*).

We consider that the reading "by those whose intellects are deluded by long-standing practice of their own tenets" (*svasiddhāntacirābhyāsavyāmugdhabalabuddhibhiḥ*) is not appropriate; rather, it should be "by those of weak intellect who are deluded" (*mugdhabalabuddhibhiḥ*).
The capacity [for action] in other cases as well is established by the same reasoning already stated.
Furthermore, those Vedāntic statements that establish a distinct Person— such as "He is the Lord of all, the Ruler of all, He governs this entire universe," and "All this is under His supervision"—
are also authoritative evidence in that regard.
Because it is the cause of a cognition that is non-doubtful and non-erroneous regarding its object;
and because, in the case of an already established entity, there is no possibility of the occurrence of either a proof or a refutation,
as determined by an examination of the fallacy of restating what is already known (*anuvāda*).

There would be a loss of validity for words whose domain is that [Brahman], because it would follow that even those words whose domain is action (kārya) would likewise lack validity; for even an action such as the fetching of fuel is indeed cognizable through other means of knowledge, since it is accepted that such an action is cognizable by another means of knowledge just like the cooking of rice.

Now, if a statement that propounds a task (kārya) concerning the Agnihotra and other rites— which are distinct from [ordinary] characteristics— is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because no other means of knowledge could possibly apprehend it, then alas! [the same would apply].

In the Blessed One, whose body is the mass of unsurpassed awakening, sovereignty, and great bliss, there is not even a trace of connection with any other means of valid cognition; thus everything is the same, except for [the fault of] dogmatic attachment.
Moreover:
Even a cognition whose object is something already perceived by another means of valid knowledge is indeed a valid cognition,
provided it does not contradict its own object as previously apprehended.
Its lack of authority arises merely from its being a matter of conceptual construction (*saṃbhāvanāmātra*), which is non-worldly (*alaukika*).

Therefore, one must accept as authoritative that cognition which is free from distinctions such as the established and the to-be-established (*pariniṣṭhita* and *iṣṭeya*), and which is neither doubtful nor erroneous; hence, this [previous position] is refuted.
As for the claim that omniscience is possible only through well-known instruments of perception and not otherwise—that is refuted by scripture itself: "He sees without eyes; he hears without ears;
he who does not see with the eye, he who sees the eyes themselves; for him there is no work."
Furthermore, the instruments [of action] exist, as do natural knowledge, power, and activity, and so forth.

Nor can these be considered figurative descriptions (*guṇavāda*), because there is no evidence for such a claim; for one resorts to figurative description only when the primary sense of a term cannot be established.
But here too, is there not a cause for abandoning the primary meaning, namely, contradiction with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?

From which other means of valid cognition? Not, first of all, from perception (*pratyakṣa*), for perception is never observed arising as a manifestor of the non-existence of the aforementioned person.

If it is argued that the certainty of non-existence arises from the non-perception of what is perceptible, we say no; for it is perceived by the scripture itself, which is the eldest in the assembly of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Nor does it arise from inference, for how could that [inference], whose logical connection (*pratibandha*) is already established by the cognition derived from scripture—which arises more swiftly—ever function?
A slow process of manifestation occurs.

Furthermore, if this were the case, the connection between sacrifices and the like with heaven, the *apūrva*, and so forth, would be contradicted by their being mere actions; yet the scripture does not invalidate that [connection].
The identity of the sacrificial post with the sun and so forth is sublated by perception itself,
because the difference between the wooden post and the solar disc is clearly perceived.
Moreover, in that case, because it forms a single syntactical unit with the injunction regarding the anointing of the sacrificial post (yūpa) present there,

it is appropriate to resort to the status of a figurative statement (guṇavāda) due to its being an explanatory passage (arthavāda); however, here there is no such other injunction of which this might be a subordinate explanatory supplement.
Now, if there were no connection with an injunction, the status of being for the sake of human purpose would be lost;
therefore, having supplied an injunction, its subsidiary character is postulated therein.
As for what they have said: "As long as words do not effect the engagement or withdrawal of cognizers, so long there is no cognition free from expectancy"— that is not correct.

For indeed, the status of being a human goal is observed even in the absence of a connection with an injunction, as in the case of "A son has been born to you" and so forth; likewise, it will be so here as well.
Nor is there an implication of an injunction (*vidhy-adhyāhāra*) in that case, because joy arises simply from the understanding of the birth of a son even without an injunction.
Likewise, this is observed in linguistic usages involving questions and answers such as "What is the action? and "Cooking."

A word that is complete in itself, having no further expectancy beyond merely conveying the specific action desired to be known by the questioner, does not require the mental supply (*adhyāhāra*) of an injunctive suffix (*vidhi*).
In this case, however, the knowledge of Brahman is heard in scripture as having the fruit of great bliss.
The knower of Brahman becomes Brahman; the knower of Brahman attains the Supreme.
That singer of the Sāmans enjoys all desires together with Brahman.
This supreme human goal of His is made manifest by the words of the three Vedas from the very beginning.

Thus, it is established that [liberation] is indeed attained in the Blessed One, who is a singular mass of auspicious qualities such as compassion and the unerring, innate, and universal direct perception acquired through hundreds of scriptural authorities as described above. It is certainly established.

The authority of the Tantra is established because it is rooted in that direct experience. Now, one might object: "Granted that, according to the logic you have set forth, there may indeed be someone who possesses innate omniscience as measured by the summit of the sacred tradition; and he..."
As long as Hari is not fully understood, the Pañcarātra certainly does not constitute valid authority.
This is far too little; for those who know the three Vedas do not dispute here that Vāsudeva is the Supreme Self and the cause of the entire universe.
Indeed, it is heard in the Upaniṣads (Vedāntas) that Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Self.
Truth, knowledge, and infinity—this is the supreme state of Viṣṇu.
"Vāsudeva is the supreme primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and likewise the presiding lord (*adhyakṣa*);
he alone is the one beyond, from whom this [universe] came into being, than whom there is nothing further, nor anything else superior.
Thus, in accordance with what is expressed [in scripture], [it is said]: "From whence indeed these beings [arise]; in the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone. (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1).

And from such statements as these, Viṣṇu—the head of the three Vedas, whose pure awakening is established—is recognized as the Supreme Self, the omniscient one; for it is heard in the Śruti that the birth, sustenance, and destruction of the universe proceed from no other than Him. Thus it is agreed.
We understand this very Supreme Self from the words of great sages such as Dvaipāyana, Parāśara, and Nārada; for instance:
"O scorcher of foes, know that the entire world is situated in Viṣṇu."
This Great Viṣṇu creates the multitude of beings, both moving and unmoving.
He draws this [world] in at every moment and emits it again;
in him all things go to their dissolution, and from him they arise once more.
"The glorious Lord Muni Nārāyaṇa is without beginning or end;
he indeed creates all beings, both stationary and moving,
and he is the supreme Brahman"— thus it is recited elsewhere as well.
"O best of the Bharatas! It is heard in many ways in the Śruti that Keśava is the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, the Puruṣa, and everything."
Thus, for those desiring to know the truth through reasons from every perspective, the truth is this:
Hari Nārāyaṇa, the Lord, is the one Great Yogin. Thus [it is said].
Likewise, regarding the duty of charity:
"The Supreme Self, the Transcendent, the Peaceful, the Lotus-navelled One, the Ultimate Refuge"—
do you not know this secret of the Vedas, O Purandara?
By his grace, we all have become the causes of stability for the worlds;
we are considered the foremost among the attendants (amaras), as well as the gods who dwell in their respective stations.
"If Viṣṇu remains indifferent, no auspiciousness exists for us"—
such are the words of Rudra, as found likewise in the Bhārata and the Mātsya Purāṇas.
"In that regard, he who is indeed the Supreme Self is eternal, devoid of qualities, and auspicious;
he should be known as Nārāyaṇa, for he is the Self of all, the Puruṣa. Thus it is said in the Varāha [Purāṇa].
Who else on earth could have possessed such conduct and vows as that deity,
except for the Lord Nārāyaṇa?
Thus:
"There has never been, nor will there ever be, a god superior to Nārāyaṇa.
This is the secret of the Vedas and the Purāṇas, O best of beings. Thus [it is said].
Likewise, in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*: "That one Supreme Person, the most excellent Janārdana, is the Paramātman;
from him comes Brahmā, from him Rudra, and from him the entire world."
Likewise: "The world has arisen from Viṣṇu and remains situated in him alone;
he is the agent of its maintenance and withdrawal"—such is the word of Parāśara.
Likewise, in the *Mānava*:
"Nārāyaṇa is beyond the unmanifest; from the unmanifest arose the cosmic egg. Within the egg are these worlds and the earth with its seven continents."
Therefore, by a thorough examination of such Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇa,
it is determined that Vāsudeva, the Supreme Self, is the cause of the entire universe;
nor has the status of being the Supreme Self been declared for Rudra and others in the Śrutis.
On the contrary, those who follow the Ekāyana branch say that it is precisely origination [that constitutes nirvana].
This is seen likewise in the Veda in passages such as "Darkness indeed was this," for it is said:
"From that Rudra was born; he is the most excellent among the worlds."
"Thus it was the eldest among the worlds"—
in this way, the state belonging to Rudra is clearly perceived as being produced by action.
"He obtained his own greatness from the worship of Viṣṇu"; "From the forehead of this god there arose a drop, and from that Rudra was born"—
such scriptural passages indeed declare the origin of Rudra.
And this being the case, [these passages] are like those that reveal the greatness of Rudra and others.
Those words which are intent upon praise, such as "The ear is Brahman," are like mere speech;
by this, the Purāṇic doctrines asserting that Rudra and others are the Supreme Self are not to be taken in their primary sense,
due to their contradiction with direct Vedic revelation (pratyakṣa-śruti).
Alternatively, those which teach the established tenets of the Tantras as things to be abandoned— indeed,
it is their greatness that is proclaimed within the non-Vedic Tantras.
In the paths of the Vedic doctrines, Viṣṇu alone is remembered as supreme. As it is said in the Vaiṣṇava [Purāṇa]:
"The Supreme Self and the Supreme Lord is the support of all."
He is celebrated by the name Viṣṇu in the Vedas and in the Vedāntas.
In the Vārāha [Purāṇa]: "Viṣṇu alone is the Supreme Brahman; he is recited here as being threefold.
Those who are deluded do not know this regarding the paths of the Vedantic tenets."
"There has never been, nor will there ever be, a god superior to Nārāyaṇa.
This is the secret of the Vedas and the Purāṇas, O best of beings. Thus it is stated in the Mātsya Purāṇa.
"In the *sāttvika* kalpas, the majesty of Viṣṇu is proclaimed; in the *tāmasa* [kalpas], the majesty of Agni and Śiva is celebrated. Thus it is said in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*.
"Indeed, no other goal whatsoever is ordained apart from Viṣṇu;
thus do the Vedas sing constantly—of this there is no doubt."
Thus it is stated in the Vāyavīya [Purāṇa]:
"The supreme Prajāpati, possessing a thousand arms,
is declared to be the Puruṣa who traverses the path of the three Vedas."
Thus it shall be:
"In the paths of the Vedic doctrines, Viṣṇu alone is remembered as the supreme;
Viṣṇu alone is the best of men, the greatest, the Supreme Person."
Thus, this entire work— entitled *Puruṣanirṇaya*,

composed by the Supreme Teacher (*Paramācārya*) and dedicated to establishing Viṣṇu as the ultimate reality by means of demonstrating the greatness of the Blessed One while distinguishing Him from other deities— is concluded.
Since this has been established more skillfully in the *Nirṇaya*, it is not elaborated upon here.
And therefore:
"It was spoken by Vāsudeva, who is renowned at the summit of the Vedas."
How can our tongue proceed to say that the Tantra is false?
For even that pleasure of the senses— such as dharma consisting of initiation and ritual service, heaven, sons, and so forth— which is directly realized through innate consciousness,
is intermingled with manifold sufferings and does not persist for very long; thus, it too [is not the ultimate goal].

Having cast themselves into the very side of suffering, those supreme sages such as Śāṇḍilya, Nārada, and others, who had gone forth from their homes for the sake of liberation, [found] the worship of Him— the sole means for attaining the unsurpassed ultimate bliss they desired— to be the realization of their own self.
It is thus determined that he composed the *Pañcarātra-saṃhitā* known as the *Avabodhinī*.
This principle does not apply to other tantras,
because it is possible for those authors to have been subject to error and the like.
For it is not possible for means of valid cognition such as perception to be the root [of this system];
moreover, those very same authorities do not accept that scripture is the root in other tantras.
Furthermore, because they propound meanings that contradict the established tenets of the Vedas,
the assumption that they are rooted in direct Vedic revelation is sublated.
Just as much that is contradictory has been spoken at length in the Māheśvara Tantra,
so too there are four kinds of followers of its path of practice for attaining success (siddhi).
Just as there are Kāpālikas, Kālāmukhas, and Pāśupatas, so too are there Śaivas;
among them, they proclaim the Kāpāla doctrine.
Through the knowledge of the six mudrās and by further retaining that very [knowledge],
the attainment of the fruit of liberation occurs, and not from the realization of Brahman.
Thus they have said:
"One who knows the reality of the six mudrās and is proficient in the supreme mudrā,
having meditated upon himself as seated upon the vulva-throne (bhagāsana), attains nirvāṇa."
Likewise: "The ear-ring, the necklace, the earring, the crest-jewel,
the sacred ash, and the sacrificial thread— these are declared to be the six mudrās."
The skull-cup and the khaṭvāṅga are proclaimed as the secondary mudrās;
one whose body is sealed by these is not born again in this world.

The Śrutis do not tolerate the notion that liberation is achieved through such meditation on the body seated upon a censured vulva-throne, accompanied by the knowledge of and the wearing of the six seals (*mudrās*). For those [Śrutis] are intended for one who has turned away from all desire for objects pertaining to this world and the next.
They declare that liberation is obtainable solely through the realization of one's identity with Vāsudeva, the cause of the entire universe, as in such passages as:
"Only by knowing Him does one transcend death; no other path for reaching [the goal] exists.
Likewise, the Kālāmukhas also [practice] the consumption of skulls, which is prohibited by all the scriptures.

Those who assert that the desired attainment of both seen and unseen results comes solely from bathing in the ashes of a corpse, consuming them, carrying a staff, placing jars of liquor, and worshipping the deity residing therein,
are indeed excluded from the Veda.
Furthermore, whatever has been stated by the Pāśupatas and Śaivas— whether contradictory, non-contradictory, similar, or obscure— that too is indeed excluded from the Veda.
Among those, this is the Pāśupata system:
Living beings are called "paśus" (bound souls), and Śiva is their lord;
for their benefit, he composed this work of five chapters.

In that regard, five categories have been explained, beginning with cause (*kāraṇa*): namely, cause, effect (*kārya*), injunction (*vidhi*), yoga, and the end of suffering (*duḥkhānta*). Furthermore, cause has been explained as being twofold: the material cause (*upādāna*) and the instrumental cause (*nimitta*).
Rudra is the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa), and his kalā is another cause.
Just as the great effect beginning with Mahat is proclaimed [to arise from Prakṛti], so too is Brahmā (Vidhi) celebrated;
he is the supreme one whose final act is the bathing in the ashes of the cremation ground, which is his secret conduct.
Yoga is said to be the concentration of the mind upon the heart preceded by the syllable Om;
liberation (apavarga) is considered the end of suffering—thus all five have been proclaimed to you.
The absolute cessation of suffering is expressed by the term *duḥkhānta*;
they consider that very state—characterized by the total destruction of all specific qualities of the self—to be liberation (*mukti*).
This same conception of God belongs to the Śaivas and others as well.
This entire conceptualization is contrary to the Vedas,
because the supreme Brahman is heard in the Śruti as both the efficient and material cause of the world,
and liberation consisting of great bliss is repeatedly heard of in various places therein.
The validity of these [scriptures] is contradicted by their mutual opposition;
they do not wait at all for the rejection of the triple Veda and the rod of punishment.

Furthermore, since the Śaivas and others conceive of stages of life and so forth that lie outside the system of castes and stages established by the Vedas, they are therefore excluded from the Vedic fold.
As they say: "Merely by entering the initiation, one becomes a Brāhmaṇa in an instant;
by undertaking the Kāpāla vow, a human being becomes an ascetic (yati)."
And it should not be argued: "How could Rudra, being so highly trustworthy, compose such a vast mass of text that lacks authoritative status?"
Nor is it logical to claim that [the cognition] is based on the recollection of a common creator, for that would lead to an over-extension;
since even the postulation of an error caused by the identity of names is possible.
And because it would contradict the Vedas, one does not fall into an over-extension [of the principle] on that account alone.
Furthermore, negligence is not entirely impossible even for Rudra and others;

or rather, since Rudra is known to be the author of delusive scriptures, it is logical that he composed such a treatise precisely for the purpose of deluding others, and thus it is not necessarily [the case that he is omniscient].
One must indeed resort to negligence;
and so it is said in the Vārāha Purāṇa:
"O Rudra, O mighty-armed one! You must indeed cause delusive scriptures to be composed."
Deceptive illusions such as sorcery, and acts of contrary conduct.
Having shown [the means], quickly manifest the fruit with little effort;
having shown it to all people, O Maheśvara, delude them swiftly!
Thus,

in that very same place, the Blessed Lord Rudra himself declared that the Śaiva and other Āgamas under discussion are outside the Veda (*vedabāhya*) and are intended for those who have strayed from the path of the Veda.
And he demonstrates that its sole purpose is to delude them:
"And for the sake of deluding those who have strayed from the path of the Vedas,
this scripture has been presented by me according to the method of the Naya-siddhānta."
From that time forward, O best of beings,
people devoted to the scriptures composed by me have not held the Vedas in high regard;
likewise, the Pāśupata and other such systems have flourished in the Kali age.

And thus, he shows that worship of oneself as the primary object— which is established in the *Pāśupata* and other tantras and is outside the Veda— is distinct from being a member of the Blessed One’s retinue.
That Vedic-outside ritual, having been described, is practiced directed toward me.
That indeed is called the Pāśupata, the most excellent, which deludes men.
"The lowest of men worship me as distinct from Viṣṇu"—
such collections of statements are not written here due to their great volume.
And it is evident that those who follow this scripture are outside the Veda;
as it says in that very same [text]:
"He cursed them, who were observers of the vows of matted hair, ashes, and skull-bowls."
You shall become outsiders to the Triple Veda, excluded from the rituals of the Vedas.
"In the Kali age, all those who bear matted hair and staffs will be of that [degenerate] nature;
they will adopt vows and dress according to their own whims and likewise wear false emblems.
Burnt by the fire of the Brahmins' curse, these devotees of Rudra will merely wear matted hair. Thus it is said.
And this is well-known in the Śaiva Āgamas:
"A rudrākṣa bracelet on the hand, a single lock of matted hair on the head,
a skull, bathing with ashes," and so forth.
And likewise, even in the Āditya Purāṇa, it describes the abandonment of the Vedas as being equal to the abandonment of the Blessed One:
"Others, endowed with ashes and matted hair, were previously described by Gautama."
They were likewise deprived of the Veda and the god Nārāyaṇa by a curse.
Thus it is said.
Furthermore, those dull-witted ones who spread such censure against Vāsudeva should be known as heretics, just as it has been declared in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*:
But those who consider the Supreme Person to be merely a universal generality (sāmānya) should indeed be known as heretics, excluded from the path of the Vedas.
Thus, and therefore:
"These very [people] do not perform even verbal worship for them;
they are heretics (pāṣaṇḍinaḥ) engaged in improper acts," as stated in the Smṛtis and other such texts.
If even the statement "those which are outside the Veda" refers to such a domain,
then [these practices] have neither the Veda as their source nor perception as their source.
It is postulated that there must be another cause [for the validity] of other tantras.
But if there were a dependence on yet another root source, then let there be a fault.
"In your system, indeed, cognition is self-validating;
yet it is precisely that validity of cognition which is being negated."
Both of these [invalidating factors] are clearly evident here through sublation and defects in the cause;
likewise, that which contradicts scripture and possesses a clearly manifest alternative basis.
Similarity by way of being a *tantra* is intended to be expressed through the example of the *Pañcarātra*;
however, similarity by way of being a ritual action (*kriyā*) exists between the killing of a Brahmin and the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
Because it is certain that both scripture and perception have their source therein;
but surely, if its source were scripture, the matter would be established from the Veda alone.
I have argued that there is no such assumption of independence for its author;
however, it is not so, for independence is indeed heard of [attributed] to a person.
"All this is under His supervision; out of fear of Him, the sun and moon stand in their courses," and so forth.

Now, if these Pañcarātra Smṛtis are indeed rooted in the Veda, why then does there not follow a recollection of the specific Vedic passages that serve as their source, just as there is a recollection of their meaning?

[This applies] to the followers of the Pāñcarātra. Nor is it reasonable to say that because the recollection of the meaning serves a purpose while the [recollection of the] text itself is fruitless, the latter should be disregarded; for it is not proper to forget that very source from which its authority derives.
Now, if it is maintained that the root of the lost Vedic recension is eternally inferable in order to account for the possibility of its being forgotten,
then whatever has been accepted by someone as authoritative would simply place that [root] at the head of his own lost recension and thereby treat it as authoritative.

Furthermore, the very existence of those two [Vedic recensions]— one eternally inferred and the other lost— is difficult to establish. If, on the other hand, those Smṛtis were indeed rooted in currently existing Vedic recensions,
then others besides their authors would likewise perceive them from those very sources.

[Objection: The effort expended in composing this treatise is futile. [Reply: To this it is said: That Blessed One is indeed the direct manifestation of the entire mass of the Vedas through unfailing innate intuition (*sahaja-saṃvedana*), consisting of various scattered injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and mantras.

Having observed that those of unsteady intellect were unable to study, retain, and so forth the many branches [of the Vedas], he, out of compassion for them, condensed their meaning by means of an easy method and taught it; thus, there is nothing at all inconsistent in this.
As they have said:
"Having extracted the essence from the Vedāntas as it is, the learned Lord Hari,
out of compassion for his devotees, has condensed [this work] for their ease."

Thus, these objections, which apply equally to all the Smṛtis beginning with that of Manu, are so easily avoided by those who have exerted themselves in the study of the Tantravārttika that they are not elaborated upon here.

But is it not the case that this claim of the *pañcarātra* tantras being rooted in the Veda is untenable, because they are seen to contain censure of the Veda? For it is said that Śāṇḍilya, finding no human goal within the four Vedas, studied this scripture.
Thus, this objection arises from a failure to understand the intended meaning of the statement; for a censure does not function merely to censure that which is censured,
but rather to praise something other than the censured, as in the case of the *Prātaranuvāka* in the *Aitareya Brāhmaṇa*.

In the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra], the statement "In the morning they speak untruth" is understood as a censure of the *homa* performed before sunrise, for the purpose of praising the *homa* performed after sunrise.
The *Ṛgveda* has the gods as its deities, whereas the *Yajurveda* is human.
The Sāmaveda, however, belongs to the ancestors; therefore, its sound is impure.
Thus, this disparagement of the Sāmaveda is for the purpose of praising the other Vedas, just as it is said in the Mahābhārata:
"The four Vedas on one side and the Mahābhārata alone on the other were formerly placed upon a scale by the assembled ṛṣis."
Because it is maintained as superior in both its greatness and its weight,
and because of its greatness and its weight, it is called the Mahābhārata.
Thus, it is understood that this is for the purpose of praising the Mahābhārata and not for censuring the Veda;
likewise, it is understood as praise for the Pañcarātra.
Furthermore, because praise for the offering of oblations before sunrise and other such acts is seen elsewhere.
In this case as well, it will be the same: the censure is not intended as the primary purpose.
The praise of the Vedas is seen many times even in the Pañcarātra: "O Lotus-Seated One, there is indeed no literary work superior to them;
this very point has been stated by the Vedāntas, which establish the knowledge of reality," and so forth.
Moreover, the phrase "in the four Vedas" does not mean that there is no human purpose (puruṣārtha) in the Vedas; rather, it means "not obtaining that human purpose which exists within them.
[Objection: But surely the grammatical connection is "not obtaining the human purpose," and not "there is no human purpose in the Vedas."
Do not say so, for there is no [such thing as] that which is to be excluded; indeed, this human goal is not found in the Vedas alone.
Therefore, one who did not find that human goal within the Vedas and desired it studied the Pañcarātra scripture; thus, there is indeed a single meaning between the Pañcarātra and the Śruti.
It is understood.
Furthermore, as for what was stated regarding those who have been consecrated by the initiatory rites of upanayana and so forth, [it is] for the purpose of propitiating the Blessed One.
The claim that [the Veda] is non-Vedic because it prescribes initiatory rites (*dīkṣā*) characterized by such purificatory ceremonies (*saṃskāra*) is incorrect;

for the *Āgnāvaiṣṇava* [offering], which prescribes initiatory rites and so forth as constituent parts of rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, is not [non-Vedic] for those who have been purified by the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) and other such rites.
A statement such as this would be non-Vedic.

Now, if the reason [for its non-Vedic status] is the prescription of a different consecration (*saṃskāra*) than the Vedic one, that is untenable; for only if the Pāñcarātra scripture were established as non-Vedic would that [reason] apply.

The establishment of its being a distinct *saṃskāra* depends on that [establishment], and the establishment of its non-Vedic nature depends on the establishment of its being a distinct *saṃskāra*; thus, there is a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*).
Furthermore, is it a distinct *saṃskāra* from all Vedic *saṃskāras*, or...

As for the cause: it cannot be the former alternative, because [the rite] does not immediately follow from a few preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*), since this would entail the consequence that even the *upanayana* and other such rites—being distinct from preparatory rites like the *caula*—would not be Vedic; nor can it be the latter alternative.

Because the aforementioned defects have not been avoided; for initiation (*upanayana*) is not established as a distinct sacrament from all Vedic sacraments, and it has already been stated that the *Pañcarātra* scripture is also Vedic, and thus its distinction from all Vedic sacraments is unproven.

As for the claim that [the Pāñcarātra] is outside the Vedic fold (*trayī-bāhya*) because it is not included among the fourteen fields of knowledge (*vidyā-sthāna*) considered authoritative for the Dharma— just like the *Pāśupata* and other tantras— that too [is refuted by] Dvaipāyana...

The argument that [the authorship] is inconclusive because of works such as the *Bhārata* and *Rāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki is incorrect; for how could the Blessed Lord Dvaipāyana have been the author of those which were refuted by the Blessed Bādarāyaṇa, who is the supreme devotee (*parama-bhāgavata*) and the mirror of all the worlds?
One might imagine that he rejects the *Bhāgavata* scripture;
for it is he who says:
"This [work] has been extracted from the extensive narrative of the *Mahābhārata*, which consists of one hundred thousand [verses]."
Having churned the churning-stick of the intellect, [the truth] was extracted like clarified butter from curd.
Just as butter from curd, as the Brāhmaṇa among bipeds,
as the Āraṇyaka from the Vedas, and as nectar from medicinal herbs.
This is the Great Upaniṣad, endowed with the four Vedas,
and proclaimed as the Pañcarātra through the final conclusions of Sāṅkhya and Yoga.
This is the highest good, this is Brahman, this is the unsurpassed benefit;
it is honored by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as by the Atharva-Āṅgirasas.
"This very instruction shall indeed be the authority," as it is stated in the Bhīṣmaparvan:
"By Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who have fulfilled their defining characteristics..."
Mādhava is to be honored, served, and worshipped.
It was sung by Saṃkarṣaṇa, following the Sātvata ritual,
at the end of the Dvāpara Yuga and the beginning of the Kali Yuga.
Thus it is said; likewise, in the Śāntiparvan as well:
"A Vaiṣṇava must certainly enter into initiation with every possible effort."
Hari is especially pleased with one who has been initiated; otherwise, he is not.
One should initiate a Brahmin in the spring, a Kshatriya in the summer,
a Vaishya in the autumn, and a Shudra in the winter.
And during the rainy season, one should [approach] a woman according to the procedure of the Pañcarātra.
Likewise:
"Measured on Mount Meru, the great mountain"— the word *samita* is derived from the word *sama* by means of the secondary suffix *itac*, and thus it carries the meaning "equal."
By hundreds of such modes of speech uttered with reverence;
How could Dvaipāyana himself refute the Pañcarātra, which is the very essence of the Vedānta and his own supreme doctrine?
How then is this sūtra [to be understood]: "Because of the impossibility of origination" (utpattyasaṃbhavāt), or what is its meaning?

This is the heart of this sūtra: since the birth of the individual soul (*jīva*) is propounded in the *Bhāgavata-śāstra*, and since that [birth] is impossible because it contradicts both scripture (*śruti*) and logic (*nyāya*), the scripture is incorrect— if this were the case...

In that case, the meaning of the Sūtra is that it is intended to refute the *Pañcarātra* scriptures; for the production of the individual soul (*jīva*) is not accepted in the *Pañcarātra* scriptures, such that this [objection] could be raised.
[Objection: But there is this statement: "Vāsudeva is the supreme primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the Supreme Self."
From that, the individual soul named Saṃkarṣaṇa is born; from Saṃkarṣaṇa, the mind known as Pradyumna is born; and from that, the ego-sense named Aniruddha is born. Thus it is said;
however, this manifestation of the Lord is proclaimed in the form of a divine array (vyūha).
In that regard, the word "jīva" is employed for the sake of conventional usage.
In order to establish the distinction of those worthy of worship according to the direct order of the castes (*varṇa*), as they have said:
"The four [deities] are to be worshipped by the four castes respectively. Furthermore:
The words *jīva*, *manas*, and *ahaṅkāra* do not denote the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), but rather designate persons possessing distinct bodies presiding over those respective [subtle elements].
Birth is designated as the acquisition of a diverse body.
Just as the words "toyena jīvāni" (I revive with water) are spoken over the head, so too is this sacrificial formula (*yajus*).

Moreover, scriptural, traditional, and popular assertions concerning the origin and dissolution of the individual soul (jīva) have already been resolved by the author of the Sūtras in the very passage: "But the designation [of the soul] as belonging to the moving and the non-moving may be figurative, because it exists when that [the body] exists" (Brahma-sūtra 2.3.16).

In the very passage, "The Self is the substratum because of the eternity [taught] by the Śruti and Smṛti," the production of the individual soul (jīva) from Brahman was already refuted on the grounds of its contradiction with Śruti, Smṛti, and logic; therefore, since that objection has been disposed of, it does not require to be raised again, and thus this would result in treating as a formal topic (adhikaraṇa) what is no longer a formal topic. By this same reasoning, [the argument] "nor [is there production] from the agent... [is also refuted].

The aphorism "the instrument" has been explained; for here it is not stated that the mind, as an instrument, originates from Saṅkarṣaṇa as its agent, since it has already been said that these words refer to a distinct Puruṣa.

If it is argued that an instrument does not arise from an agent because we do not observe an axe or similar instruments arising from an agent such as Devadatta, then alas, you have destroyed the very Brahman who is established in its own majesty, being devoid of the entire collection of instruments!
The acceptance of the production of all the instruments, beginning with the vital breath (prāṇa) and the mind (manas), as expressed in the passage,
"From this [Self] are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs," is accepted exactly as it is, because it is well-established by scripture (śruti).
O sir, why do you not accept this, given that it is well-established in the Pañcarātra?
Indeed, the abandonment of a meaning well-established by tradition is not at all commendable;
for the validity of both is equal, since they arise from faultless cognition.
As for these four, are they sharers in equal sovereignty? Or are they independent, or rather the fourfold manifestation of the body of one [Lord] according to his own will?

Having thus deliberated: "If they share equal sovereignty, there can be no state of being an effect because of their equality. If it is argued that one [Lord] is a differentiation of forms, what purpose is served by such a distinction?"
Thus it has been explained that [the opponent] objects by saying, "Or, if there were the existence of consciousness and so forth, there would be no negation of that.
That is incorrect, because such an alternative is impossible; for indeed—
A certain proponent of theism has accepted a world with multiple lords,
particularly the Pāñcarātrikas, who assert that Vāsudeva alone is the single supreme primordial nature;
however, they maintain that this very Blessed One, manifesting in four distinct forms as a matter of divine play, protects the entire universe.

Nor is this untenable, for it is logically consistent— just like the manifestation of Balarāma, Bhīṣma, Arjuna, and others— since it is exactly as with the Lord’s own pastimes, wherein the entire manifold world consisting of ether, wind, Śiva, Brahmā, and so forth, is fashioned.

For one whose sole purpose is inconceivable and of great majesty, the voluntary incarnations as Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, Śatrughna, and others will not be contradictory; likewise, it is the same with the distinctions of Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and so forth.

As for the phrase "because of contradiction" (*yatparaṃ vipratiṣedhāt*), it refers either to the contradiction with the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) in the passage "in the four Vedas," or to the mutual contradictions among the Tantras themselves. Regarding the claim that they are "not authoritative," the contradiction with the Vedic revelation has already been employed [earlier]; as for the mutual contradiction, however—
For treatises (*tantra*) whose verbal expressions are established through the principles of primary factors, qualities, universals, particulars, and so forth, there is indeed certainty;
however, for words devoid of the support of such principles, there is no certainty whatsoever. As it has been said regarding the expression established by the principles: [text continues].

Or rather, it is that which subsequently conveys the meaning of the sentence; therefore, by means of such statements as "this Mahopaniṣad," the author of the Sūtras has [established] its authority as being particularly more esteemed than that of the Vedas.

To explain the Sūtra as being intended to refute [the Pañcarātras] by superimposing upon them a doctrine of the production of the individual soul (jīva) which does not exist in the Pañcarātra Tantras, reveals nothing but the [ignorance] of the commentators themselves; enough of this prolixity.

In this regard, the meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: having previously established the inconsistency of the systems of Kapila, Kāśyapa, Sugata, and Paśupati— the opponents of our own intended doctrine—
on the grounds of their contradiction with Śruti and Nyāya, [the author] now...

Fearing that even the *Pañcarātra* tantras intended by [the author] themselves might be suspected of inconsistency— just like other systems— due to their being enumerated alongside them in the intellect (i.e., because they are categorized together with other doctrines),
he establishes their authority (the meaning of which is "by the logic of driving in a pillar"; for just as a pillar...)

Desiring to make it firm, they themselves move it with their hand and examine it. It is thus explained: therein, by the first two sūtras, the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) is introduced; for instance:
The Pañcarātra scripture is not authoritative because of the impossibility of origination; that is, because the origination of Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others which it propounds is impossible.
How is it impossible? Because it is untenable in either way. To explain:
However, these four alone share in equal sovereignty;
or there may be one in the fourfold division, for a twofold derivation is impossible.
If they possess equal sovereignty, then because of their equality, one would not create at all;
even if a single selfhood is accepted, such production is impossible,
for the distinction between creator and created cannot logically exist within a single entity.

Likewise, there can be no instrument from an agent; for this reason as well, [the scripture] is not authoritative, because it is impossible for the mind, known as Pradyumna, to arise from the agent known as Saṅkarṣaṇa, who is the individual soul (jīva). Indeed, an axe does not arise from Devadatta.

Or rather, the instrument does not arise from the agent; for, following from this, the instrument is not produced from Saṃkarṣaṇa, who is the agent, because scripture declares that the origin of all instruments proceeds from Brahman alone, as in the passage:
"From Him are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the senses. Or else, [the instruments arise] from the state of consciousness and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "there is no refutation of that," the word "or" (vā) reverses the position [of the opponent].
As for what was stated— that there is a lack of authority because the production of Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others is impossible in either case— that is not so.
There is no denial of the production of that [unmanifest] from Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others.
For if these—consciousness and the rest—did not exist, there would be a denial of production.
And consciousness is the "beginning" (it is taken up, appropriated, and employed).

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of all purposes" and so forth: Brahman is the cause of the entire world. Although, according to Pāṇini’s rule *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ*, the word *ādi*—ending in the suffix *ki*—would necessarily be neuter, nevertheless, in this context, its masculine gender should be understood as being established by means of an *auṇādika* (derivative) suffix.

Since it has been taught exactly thus by the rule "In the usage of the learned, [words] such as *saṃjñās* are forms of verbal roots" (*śiṣṭaprayoge saṃjñāsu dhāturūpāṇi*), and since the usage of the learned is itself the root of the teaching of the learned, one may assume that [the word] *puṃs-* belongs exclusively to the non-ṛk-ṇādi group.
Alternatively, the reading is simply *vijñānam cādir ca*; and from that, *vijñānam*...

The term *cādi* is a collective dvandva compound meaning "consciousness and so forth. Even in ancient manuscripts, the word *vijñāna* appears without the visarga in the compound *vijñānādi* precisely due to the confusion arising from observing the form resulting from that collective dvandva formation.

Some believe that when "and so forth" (*cādi*) was intended [to be mentioned], the authors wrote "consciousness and so forth" (*vijñānaṃ cādi*). It is precisely because of this lack of satisfaction that the teachers of the text adopted an alternative interpretation; and in this very same way, the investigation of the doubt and its resolution occurs in the *Śrībhāṣya* on the Sūtra concerning consciousness and the rest (*vijñānādi-sūtra*).

Others say that this was done through a deceptive fabrication of words; however, in reality, in the *Śrībhāṣyakośa* and the *Āgamaprāmāṇyakośa*, it is generally found—without dependence on any specific region—that in the *Vijñānādi-sūtra* (*vijñānaṃ cādi ca vijñānādi*; Brahman is that state), [the term "Brahman" occurs].

Thus, this alone is the authoritative reading; therefore, that usage must necessarily be explained through a specific intended meaning (*tātparya-viśeṣa*), and not according to its literal sense, such as the word *ādi* (and so forth), which would have a final meaning common to non-Brahmanical sources. Regarding this very point, we explain as follows: *ā* means "all around" (*samantāt*), and *attu*...
In the phrase "śīlam asya" (this is his habit), the suffix *ṇini* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule *supyajātau ṇinistācchīlye*,
which prescribes *ṇini* in the sense of habitual character (*tācchīlya*). Furthermore, what is intended here is its exclusivity (*asādhāraṇya*),

and this is to be understood in accordance with the method explained in the *Adhikaraṇa* [of the Brahma Sūtras] beginning with "Because of the mention of the moving and the unmoving, He is the Eater."
By the phrase "the action unique to Brahman" and similar terms,

the Supreme Brahman— the agent of the devouring of the entire universe— is denoted; and by the word "knowledge" (*vijñāna*), it is indicated that this [action] should not be considered a property of *pradhāna* as asserted in the systems of Sāṅkhya and others.
It is thus distinguished. And so, in the sūtra "That from which there is the origin, etc., of this," since the cause of the world's maintenance and destruction is intended by the word "etc.
(*ādi*) as part of the definition, when establishing the difference from others by means of that definition, the three—origin and the rest—are the causes acting in combination.
Since the causality of each [term] individually must be stated due to the lack of pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*),

Brahman is presented by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in its own specific form; and this being so, [the compound *vijñānādi* is analyzed as] "Brahman, which is both consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth."
For certain individuals who grasp the literal meaning [of the texts], the fact that the names of the Śrībhāṣya teachers and their supreme teacher, the venerable Yāmunamuni,
are clearly and appropriately stated is itself the basis for their failure to understand the intent of these teachers, resulting in the perception of inconsistency.

Here, however, others—having applied the suffix *kvip* by virtue of [the root] being listed in the *saṃpad-ādi* group, having then applied [another suffix] in the sense of the same meaning (*svārthe*), and having established the form *āda*, subsequently seek to establish the word *ādin* by means of the possessive suffix *ini*. This too, being struck down by the prolixity of its derivation, does not lead to the complete satisfaction of the learned. Furthermore:

Since the word *accha*—derived from the root *ac* with the suffix *kvip* in the sense of *saṃpad* and others—is invariably feminine, the suffix *aṇ* would necessarily follow; and because it ends in *aṇ*, the suffix *ṅīp* would inevitably occur, resulting in the form *ācchī*. Therefore, even in that case, there is no possibility of achieving the desired result. Furthermore, as for the derivation *āda* meaning "eating" according to the rule [Pāṇini 3.3.18] regarding the abstract sense (*bhāve*).

Having formed the noun *bhāva* by means of the suffix *ghañ*, and having derived *ādi* from that *bhāvaghañanta* form by adding the possessive suffix *ini*, this [derivation] is based on a forgetfulness of the Pāṇinian rule *ghañapośca*. This is because [the rule] applies when *ghañ* is present.

Because of the prescription of the substitution of *ghas* [for the root *ad*], and because of the understanding that Brahman consists of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth, there is no prohibition against arising—that is, arising into the state of Brahman—when that state of Brahman exists.
This is what is meant: of the one Supreme Self alone...
The relationship of cause and effect is established for Vāsudeva, whose power is unlimited, by virtue of his immersion in his own *māyā*.
As for the claim that the mind (*manas*) does not arise from Saṅkarṣaṇa because scripture speaks of its arising from Brahman alone—
That too has been refuted by [the fact that it arises] as consciousness and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "the instrument does not arise from the agent," what is being said? Does it mean that whatever is the instrument of a particular action does not arise from the agent of that action, or that [it does not arise] from any agent whatsoever?
Or [the second alternative is]: "That instrument does not arise from any agent whatsoever.

Regarding these, in the first case, the inference is contradicted by the fact that it proves what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*); for in this context, the mind—which is arising from the agent Saṅkarṣaṇa—is not an instrument for its own production.
Because it is an object (*karman*), nor because it is the agent (*kartṛ*) in its own production.

Furthermore, in another alternative, there is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa-vipratiṣedha*), since we observe the production of jars and other things— which serve as instruments (*karaṇa*)— from an agent such as a potter, even when they are used for purposes like fetching water.
This is what he means by the phrase "because of contradiction. Alternatively, another explanation of this pair of sūtras is stated:
[the opponent's position] is joined with the existence of the reason for the validity of cognition and so forth.
The rejection of the *Pañcarātra* as a valid authority is due to the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*);
in that case, it would result in the characteristics of mere restatement (*anuvāda*), doubt, and the non-arising of knowledge.
The lack of authority [of the Veda] has been refuted here by the inclusion of the term "cognition" (vijñāna),
in order to dispel the suspicion of falsity that might arise based on the intention of the speaker.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it is intended to express that the tantras were spoken by a reliable authority (*āpta*). For instance:
"He who always perceives the entire world through innate intelligence (*sahaja-buddhi*)."
He who, when fully gratified by meditation alone, bestows the desired objects of men.
How could defects such as delusion or deception possibly exist in Him, whom those who have mastered the three Vedas declare to have eternally attained all desires?
The impossibility of the origination of the forms beginning with Saṃkarṣaṇa, which was stated in the two preceding sūtras, is here refuted.
"Because of contradiction" means because of the contradiction with the direct perception of the Blessed One as inferred from the *Pañcarātra* tradition,
or because of the contradiction with the *Śruti* as inferred therefrom.
Alternatively, since the sūtras are intent on demonstrating the underlying logic (*nyāya*),
they deliberate here in such a manner even by positing a non-existent contradiction between the *Pañcarātra* and the Śruti;
for if there is no contradiction with the Veda, what need is there to mention [the authority of] the words of Manu and others?
When there is doubt as to whether this treatise is authoritative or not authoritative, [it is said:]
It is invalid because it is impossible for a cognition of a contradictory object to arise;
and this impossibility is caused by the factors of dependence and independence.
For as long as the recollection of the *Pañcarātra*, being dependent [on other means],

does not begin to cognize its own object by way of establishing a primary means of valid cognition (*mūlapramāṇa*), so long will the meaning of that [recollection] be otherwise [established] through a conviction arising from an independent, authorless scripture (*apauruṣeyāgama*).
Because it is impossible for a valid cognition contrary to that [Pāñcarātra] to arise through such a determination;
for the Pāñcarātra’s comprehension of its foundational Śruti persists only so long as its root is not severed by the weapon of the scripture of direct perception (pratyakṣa-śāstra).

Now, one might object: how can the Vedas be independent, given that their status as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇatva*) is likewise dependent upon the experience of the Blessed Lord, since He is their cause? For just as the *Smṛtis* of the Pañcarātra depend upon His experience, so too do the Vedas.

To this it is replied: "And there is no instrument of the agent"—that is, the Vedas are not an instrument (karaṇa) of the agent, the Lord; for they are called an instrument in the sense that "they are made" (*kriyante*), the suffix *lyuṭ* being used in the passive sense (*karmani*). This means, in short, that the Vedas are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*). Alternatively, if [the opponent argues] that they exist as a state of higher knowledge (*vijñāna*) and so forth, then that [status of being an instrument] is not denied; provided, however, that such [human authorship] does not exist.

The *Pañcarātra-śāstra* is not invalid; rather, its non-refutation means that there is no refutation of the arising of valid cognition. The meaning is that even contradictory portions are authoritative through alternative application (*vikalpena*).
Because it is rooted in the experience of one who is free from error and deception,
when there is the state of "vijñāna" and so forth, "vijñāna" means distinguished knowledge— that is to say, knowledge in which no failure is possible; for others...

The knowledge of those who compose treatises on all the dharma-śāstras is subject to various failures, because it pertains to the realm of saṃsāra, is not omniscient, and involves unfulfilled desires;
however, the knowledge of the Blessed One possesses natural and unrestrained sovereignty.

The knowledge that consists of the direct realization of all phenomena— such as dharma and adharma— which are innate and non-erroneous, and which is attained through hundreds of scriptural revelations,
is called *vijñāna*. In this context,
the term *vijñānādibhāva* is a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the primordial state of such *vijñāna*."
It should be understood that since it exists as the primary state and the root [of knowledge], there is no negation of it; rather, it is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Now, how can the authority of a *tantra* that contradicts the *Śruti* be accepted?
For if it were authoritative, an option (*vikalpa*) with the *Śruti* would result, and such an option—
It is corrupted by eight defects; yet,

because there is no reason to abandon either one in certain cases, it is permitted out of necessity, as in the injunctions "one should sacrifice with rice" and "one should sacrifice with barley," for in those instances it is not possible to set aside either alternative.
Because both are equally independent [of external authority].
Nor does it follow that there must be an option between the Pañcarātra and the Veda even on this basis, because they are not equal;
for a Vedic statement is independent due to its being authorless (apauruṣeya), whereas [the other] is dependent.
If it is said that [the authority] belongs to the words of the Pañcarātra, how can there be an option between these two?
Listen: it is precisely because the Pañcarātra scripture is independent [of other means of knowledge].
But how can there be independence for a human utterance?
If this is so, let this logician explain it when he is questioned.
Is its dependence on another accepted for the sake of making it known,
or for the sake of determining it, or for the sake of communicating it as it truly is?
Or rather, even the four [means] are impossible there for the sake of human goals; indeed,
this statement being heard— "one should worship the Blessed One with the metaphorical designation of a universal monarch"— requires nothing else for its comprehension.

This is because it involves the acquisition of proficiency; nor does it follow that it is weak due to its dependence on other factors, for if that were so, even the Vedic revelation (śruti) would be subject to weakness.
Nor is it for the sake of producing certainty, for [the word] "one should worship" does not mean "should one worship or not?"
It produces a cognition that is subject to doubt, because this would entail the contradiction of both its origination and its comprehension.
Nor does it serve for the sake of truthfulness; for a cognition once produced does not depend on anything else—such as a "quality" (*guṇa*)—beyond its own causes in order to be true.
Because validity is untenable and because it is not admitted [by us],
nor is there dependence on another for the sake of human purpose,
since that is established merely by examining the very body of the scripture; for here—
It is understood from the scripture itself that for those possessing the aforementioned purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), there arises knowledge of the meaning of the scripture through its study;
from that, the performance of the five-fold daily observances (*pañcakālika-anuṣṭhāna*) regarding that meaning follows; and from that, the attainment of unsurpassed prosperity (*niratiśaya-saṃpat*).

Now, if it should be argued that even though the *Pañcarātra* tantras possess intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), their validity is not established as long as the absence of defects is not ascertained by first determining the reliability of their speaker— that is incorrect; for it is not the case that the knowledge of the absence of defects [is required].
It establishes validity because that [validity] arises solely from the cause of faultless cognition.

Nor is there a requirement for the ascertainment of qualities such as being an authoritative person (*āpta*) for the sake of faultlessness, since that [validity] is established by their mere existence;
as the author of the *Vārttika* has said: "But at that time, they do not function..."

"Qualities [are required] by virtue of being known. Thus, it has been shown that even in the cognition of the absence of defects, qualities serve through their mere existence; for when the absence of defects is to be cognized, they assist by their mere presence. And yet, even though a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has arisen...
One does not require anything further for the conventional activities of rejection, acquisition, and so forth, since these are established through memory and desire alone; as they have said:
"Conventional activity proceeds from memory and from desire."
Moreover, even for the Vedas, which possess intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*),

their authority is not established until the absence of defects is ascertained through a prior determination of the existence of an author; thus, the state of being dependent [on external factors] is the same.

Now, if it is argued that since the existence of a speaker is established without effort through the very non-perception of what is suitable [to be perceived], defects lacking a substratum are impossible, and thus there is no suspicion of invalidity regarding the Veda at all—
as they have said:
In that regard, the exclusion of [the charge of] sublation is easier to establish because of the existence of a speaker;
therefore, the lack of authority in the Veda does not even give rise to suspicion.

Thus, alas! In that case, since the absence of defects is established without effort in the Pañcarātra Tantra as well— precisely because it was spoken by the omniscient and omnipresent Lord— the suspicion of invalidity does not even arise.
The discussion is the same.

This is what is meant: for both [types of cognition] that possess intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*), the ascertainment of the absence of defects in one case arises from the ascertainment of the absence of the person who is the locus of those defects; in the other case, it is likewise.
This is because there is a certainty regarding the speaker possessing qualities contrary to that [assertion].

For example, the certainty of the absence of heat in the sky arises from the certainty of the absence of its substratum; however, in the case of water, it arises from the perception of coldness, which is contrary to it.
Furthermore:
Dependence and independence are not indeed the cause of sublation;
for the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is the sublater of that [cognition] which is independent.
This cognition of silver is not admitted to be dependent upon that [silver];
for this perception "this is a flame" arises from the destruction of the oil and the wick.
Inference is seen to be subversive even when it depends upon that which is born of the senses;
therefore, that which has scope is negated by that which lacks scope.
In this matter, there is no room for conflict between the teachings of the Blessed One and the Vedas;
however, it is difficult [to reconcile] those portions of the Tantra that contradict the Śruti.
