If you think that [the authorship] must be determined as being composed by Vāsudeva,
how could this apply to a portion of the Veda that contradicts the Pañcarātra?
The cognition that [the Veda] is not of human origin arises as sublated;
since that too is a part of the Veda, its status as such is accepted.
Since this [Veda] also consists of five nights (pañcarātra), let it be accepted that it was composed by him;
for if it were claimed to be of non-human origin (apauruṣeya) because its author is not remembered, [then the same would apply here].
Why should its authorship not be established here by the tradition of its being composed by him?
For there exists, from the time of the seers down to children, that firm succession of tradition.
"Keśava, the Blessed One, is the author of the Pañcarātra;
because of my conviction that it was composed by him, [I gave] many elephants, horses, and wealth."
Having given various sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), they perform the consecration and other rites;
Kapila is the teacher of Sāṅkhya, and Keśava is the teacher of Pañcarātra.
Thus it is recited in the Skanda Purāṇa as well as in the Bhārata:
"Nārāyaṇa himself is the speaker of the entire Pañcarātra."
This is the Great Upaniṣad, endowed with the four Vedas,
and proclaimed as the Pañcarātra through the final conclusions of Sāṅkhya and Yoga.
O dear one! Nārada caused the Munis to hear that which had issued from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa in the abode of Brahmā, exactly as it was seen and exactly as it was heard.
Thus, by means of thousands of arguments set forth in the Purāṇas and supported by logic,
the fact that the Pañcarātra was composed by Vāsudeva is established beyond doubt.
However, while scholars dispute the eternity of the Veda,
both [the Veda and the Buddha] are equally the cause of faultless knowledge.
The authority of the Blessed One’s scripture and the Veda is beyond doubt;
therefore, because they are equally refined, their authority is established as an option.
Thinking thus, the high-minded author of the Sūtras declares:
"Or, if [the pradhāna] exists as consciousness and so forth, there is no refutation of it."

But surely, even though error is considered impossible for the Blessed One due to his omniscience, he might still deceive others because of his omnipotence; so was this scripture spoken in order to delude them, or rather, with a mind truly attentive to the truth?
For those whose minds are distressed by having to resort to one side or the other regarding what is "established" (nibaddha), what indeed could be the means of reaching a definitive conclusion?
On the contrary, we determine that this results only in confusion, precisely because it contradicts the Veda.

To this it is replied: "Because of contradiction," meaning that if there were a suspicion of subversion based merely on the Lord's omnipotence without any cause, it would contradict all the Śrutis, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and the world.
Alas! If, because of his omnipotence, he were to cast even the righteous into hell, the world would fall into a state of paralysis due to the resulting doubt.
Moreover, this [being], desiring to deceive by means of his omnipotence,
having first created the Vedas— which contain unperceivable and false objects—
further deprived Hiraṇyagarbha and others even of their power to remember their own creation, and from that time onward...

"How can we have confidence, when we are beset by doubt as to whether or not he initiated this tradition of Vedic study? Furthermore, even though he possesses all powers, there is no evidence that he would exercise them to the full extent; for such exercise would lead to an infinite regress, and because the Blessed One has naturally attained all his desires."

Because it is free from even a trace of defects such as partiality and cruelty due to the absence of any motive for deception, and because it is established in its natural benevolence toward all classes of living beings, it would be impossible for the wise to have been deceived by it up until this day, were it composed for the purpose of deceiving.

If it is argued that such a doubt does not arise for those who engage in the study of their own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*) and the performance of its prescribed duties— since it is impossible for them to forget the defects of the author of such a work— then all of this is equally applicable elsewhere as well.
For instance:
what purpose could there be for this one who has attained all desires, who is omniscient, and who is a treasury of compassion,
with those of little strength who have failed to attain their goals and have been deceived?
How could the supreme sages, whose heads are equal to the Vedas, have composed a Tantra for deception, or why would they praise it here and there with such uniformity?

For indeed, in the Vārāha, Rāmāyaṇa, Mahābhārata, and other works, virtuous people declare that this Tantra possesses a secret nature no different from the Vedas; we shall explain this very point. (The Dravidian reading says they "read" [it].)
O twice-born one, I am attainable through Vedic knowledge, through the Pañcarātra, through devotion, and through sacrifice;
I am not attainable otherwise, even in hundreds of lakhs of years.
If anyone should take up [this] for five thousand nights,
and if there should be someone who is my devotee at the exhaustion of their karma;

The Vedas and the Pañcarātra will eternally dwell within his heart; when [the time] has arrived, they shall remain there—this is the teaching of the Ṛṣis. This scripture of mine, the Pañcarātra, is most difficult to obtain.
By my grace, you shall undoubtedly come to know all of this—
through the Purāṇas, the Vedas, and likewise the Pañcarātra.

Yogins meditate upon Him constantly, and they worship Him with sacrifices. Thus, O best of beings, Sāṅkhya, Yoga, the Vedas, the Āraṇyakas, and the Pañcarātra are all mutually constituent parts of one another.
He who perceives through the Veda in five nights—he truly sees;
this is the Great Upaniṣad, endowed with the four Vedas.
I shall desist from such words as these, for they are endless;
yet, if you still fear the corruption of a treatise of this nature.
"There would be no confidence in anything whatsoever"— this is taught because of contradiction;
and thus it is so.
Even if there were a contradiction between the scripture of the Blessed One and the Vedas, there would be an option [to choose one];
however, I have already demonstrated previously that no such contradiction exists at all.
Now, it may be asked: "Is it not the case that by the title 'Bhāṣyakāra' (Commentator) here, the venerable Dramiḍācārya is intended?
For the venerable Śrī Rāmānujācāryas, the authors of the Śrībhāṣya, were disciples of the disciples of the venerable Yāmunamuni. [Thus ends the portion of] the Śrībhāṣya...

Since it was composed at a later time than the venerable Sage Yāmunamuni, that commentary cannot be intended here. How indeed could there be a statement regarding the authority of contradictory portions, even if a contradiction exists?
Having considered this, [the author] avoided it; yet even that was solely for the purpose of ensuring that those of tender minds— who have plunged into the ocean of profound logic—
should not harbor a lack of respect for the Vedas, just as was the case with the venerable Jaimini.
The presentation of the fruits of action is for the purpose of increasing faith in karma.
If it was argued that [the Purāṇas] lack authority because they were accepted by those outside the Veda,
then why would the Vedas themselves not likewise lack authority because they were accepted by those outside [the Veda]?
Moreover:
What is this "being outside the Veda," and what would its "being accepted by that" mean?
Is it the case, my friend, that being outside the Veda is defined simply as being other than the Veda?
Is it the performance of prohibited acts, or a disposition of hatred toward them?
Likewise, let it be considered whether [the person] has accepted [the teaching], studied it, or understood it.
Or if the reason were the state of being currently performed, it would be faulty in all cases.
In that regard, first of all:
if being external means being distinct from the Veda, then that [quality of] having been studied would also apply;
for a Vedic statement might be studied by three castes other than those [to whom it is traditionally restricted].
In that case, it follows that the reason [for your argument] is inconclusive because it is itself a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Even if it were known or apprehended, you are not released from this fault;
for if its purpose were merely that which is being performed, then the previously mentioned state of being outside the Veda would remain.
Even if they were accepted by the Vedas, there would likewise be inconsistency regarding the performance of prohibited acts,
which is the defining characteristic of being outside the Vedic fold.
There is no contradiction with the Vedic statements that prescribe expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*);

for those scriptural passages prescribing expiation— such as "one should offer oblations with the *kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras"— have as their very purpose the performance of actions that have been studied and undertaken by those who have committed prohibited acts.
The reason "being accepted by those outside the Veda" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to [their] being valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Nor is there a lack of authority for the *Pañcarātra* tantras simply because they are accepted by people who hate the Veda, since the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*); moreover, it is not so.

Acceptance by those who hate the Veda destroys its authority; for if it were not to destroy it, then the path of the nihilists would be unobstructed, as they indeed strive to subvert the authority of the Veda.
By some means, having seized Vedic sentences through deception,
the Digambaras could easily render the Vedas false in their meaning.

If it is argued that there is no fault in the faultless Vedic sentences because of the consideration of such statements as, "Now, one should not utter [the Veda] even for those students who are unqualified for it,
except for the offering of *svadhā* to the ancestors," and so forth;

This same defect applies to those listeners who lack qualification even for those tantras currently under discussion, but not to those tantras that are themselves free from defects; thus, everything is the same except for the matter of personal attachment (*abhiniveśa*). Now, if it is thought that "being outside the Veda" means a lack of qualification for Vedic rituals—
Because it has been adopted by those outside the Veda who lack authority [to practice it], it is invalid, like the formula for bowing to a *caitya*. In that regard as well,
is the reason the fact that it has been accepted by people who lack authority for any Vedic ritual whatsoever, or...

Having analyzed the claim that [the Smṛtis] were accepted by certain Vedic Kāma-ras who lacked authority, please explain it. First of all, the former alternative is not tenable because the reason is unestablished (hetvasiddhi);
for there is no such person among humans who has ever been engaged in any Śrauta rite.
One should not grant [the status of] non-violence and so forth to mere humanity;

for otherwise, even those such as Caṇḍālas who commit the killing of Brahmins, the theft of their property, sexual union with women of the [higher] castes, the study of the Vedas, and so on, would [be entitled to these].
[They] would incur sin, because they lack the qualification for it; for when one performs that which ought not to be performed by him, it leads to transgression.
Therefore, since the qualification for such Vedic rites exists for all [persons], the reason (hetu) is unestablished (asiddha), and the example (dṛṣṭānta) is devoid of the probans (sādhanavikala).
Nor can the lack of authority be attributed to the fact that it was accepted by those who are ineligible for certain Vedic rites,
for that would entail the consequence of all Vedic sentences lacking authority; indeed, [this ineligibility] exists for everyone.
There is a lack of qualification for certain Vedic rites, as in the case of a Brāhmaṇa in the Rājasūya sacrifice or a Kṣatriya in the drinking of Soma; therefore,
the reason [adduced] is inconclusive because it is based on Vedic statements accepted by those whose eligibility is restricted to specific castes.
And it is not the cause [of falsity]:
"The notion that heaven results from the worship of a shrine is not false because of its acceptance [by others], but rather because of a defect in its cause."
And it has been stated that [the Pañcarātra] is accepted by the great sages, such as Bhṛgu, Bharadvāja, and Dvaipāyana— the foremost among all the orthodox Vaidika āstikas— and even today,
the construction of temples is carried out according to the path prescribed in the Pañcarātra tantras.

We observe that cultured people (śiṣṭas) perform such acts as the consecration of images, prostration, circumambulation, and festivals with the conviction that they are more conducive to spiritual welfare than even the Agnihotra and other rites explicitly enjoined by the direct Veda; nor is it reasonable to claim that this practice is without foundation.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even the performance of the eightfold twilight prayers (*sandhyāvandana*) and so forth would be rendered rootless; for it has been stated:
"Or rather, when no [specific] cause is perceived, those practices employed by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) should be understood as authoritative."

Now, if the reason is "because it is accepted by the devotees of the Lord" (bhāgavata-jana), then alas, it would follow that the Vājasaneyaka, the Ekāyana-śākhā, and even direct perception and other means of knowledge would be invalid, since they too are accepted by them.
Now, if the reason is "because it is accepted by those very [people]," that is both inconclusive due to being uncommon (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*) and unestablished (*asiddha*). Or,
if it is argued that it lacks authority because of being accepted by them due to their being outside the three castes (*atraivarṇikatva*), then what [is the consequence]?

O you who hold that the authority of the Atharvanic utterances— such as "The Rathakāra should perform the consecration" and "With this [rite], one should cause the Niṣāda-sthapati to sacrifice"— which have their objects performed by those other than the three [twice-born] castes, such as the Rathakāra and the Niṣāda, does not exist.
Granted that the acceptance of those belonging to other castes might be a cause for invalidity,

yet the supreme Brahminhood of these Bhāgavatas who follow the teachings of the Blessed One is established by all means of valid cognition; therefore, their acceptance only strengthens the validity [of the tradition].
He asked: "By what means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is their status as Brahmins understood, or by what means that of others?
Is it not the case that immediately upon opening one's eyes, [one perceives] the topknot (śikhā), the sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta)..."

Seeing young brahmin boys carrying staffs of *pālāśa* wood and wearing girdles of *mauñja* grass, people recognize them as Brahmins; or rather, what need is there for this, when they are seen here day after day studying the *Vājasaneyaka-ekāyana* recension?
Seeing learned men who possess shining sacred threads, upper garments, and topknots, and who are teaching, officiating at sacrifices, or receiving gifts,
people do not fail to recognize them as Brahmins. Now,
regarding [the signs of] officiating at sacrifices, teaching, the palāśa staff, and so forth—

Since deviation from the norm is possible among wicked Śūdras and others, and since [the practice] proceeds on the assumption that their Brāhmaṇahood is already established, no determination of Brāhmaṇahood can be reached through them; this applies equally to other Vipras who are not Bhāgavatas.
Now, even if there is some deviation in those cases, if one suspects deviation elsewhere on the grounds of their similarity,

that would lead to an infinite regress— just as there is suspicion of deviation regarding cognitions of silver in actual silver because of the deviation found in the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl— and because it would contradict direct perception.
The certainty regarding the state of being [so] in examples where deviation is not perceived is the same in other cases as well.
Now, it may be thought that the Brahminhood of others [is established in this way].
As for the argument that "this is because of the recollection of a lineage (gotra) not common [to all]," that applies equally to the Bhāgavatas as well;
for the Bhāgavatas indeed recollect: "We are Bhāradvājas," "We are Kāśyapas," "We are Gautamas," and "We are Aupagavas."
Nor is this recollection of lineage baseless or recent, for if it were, it would follow that all recollections of lineages are likewise [unreliable].
If there is doubt because of the possibility of defects in the genealogies, [then...]
Therefore, having attained the status of a Brahmin, he would then throw the entire world into turmoil.

For instance: "O best of virtuous men, how can you, having conceived the suspicion that your mother was an adulterer and thus harboring the doubt that you are a Caṇḍāla, recite the Veda so confidently and without hesitation?"

Therefore, since the Brahminhood of the Bhāgavatas remains unrefuted— being established by the recollection of their various lineages obtained through an uninterrupted succession— there is no difference whatsoever between the Brahminhood of the Bhāgavatas and that of others.

If, at most, those who are single-mindedly devoted have taken refuge in the Supreme Person alone, while others are worshippers of petty deities— whom the Blessed One himself has censured, saying, "But they [the commoners], O Kaunteya, sacrifice to me alone, though not according to the prescribed rule"— then what need is there to speak of these?

Whatever authority has been stated regarding Brahminhood for others, by whom was their Brahminhood understood? Is the burden of defining Brahminhood not mine alone, but rather belongs to both of us together?

The sense is that they are equal insofar as both are objects of investigation (*nirūpaṇīyatva*). By this [it is meant]: "And if there is curiosity, let it be heard what determines Brahminhood in both cases—whether it be perception, inference, or even presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)."

Now, how does perception bring about the cognition of Brahminhood? For it is not the case that immediately upon the first contact of the sense-organ with two physical bodies— similar in age, dress, and form, yet previously unseen as either a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya— one perceives [the distinction] as one does between a goat and a buffalo.
We recognize [the distinction] through differentiation, thinking "this is a Brāhmaṇa" and "this is a Kṣatriya.

Nor is it correct to say that the sense organ itself, which apprehends the Brāhmaṇahood residing in the present individual, does so independently of the recollection of the Brāhmaṇahood of his ancestors and so forth.
For that memory is untenable in the absence of a prior experience, being like the recollection of the son of a barren woman;
nor can it arise from inference, because no inferential mark (liṅga) concomitant with it is perceived.

Furthermore, tranquility, self-restraint, austerity, purity, and so forth are not the defining marks (*liṅga*) of Brahminhood, because these must be accomplished by one who is already a Brahmin and because they are subject to deviation.
Nor can Brahminhood be determined through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), as there is no logical inconsistency [without it]; nor indeed...

The determination of Brāhmaṇahood [in the injunction] "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires in spring" occurs because the meaning of such a sentence would otherwise be untenable; for the comprehension of the meaning of that sentence is preceded by the comprehension of the meanings of its constituent terms, such as "Brāhmaṇahood. This is not a fault, for indeed...

There is a rule that only that which appears at the very moment of the first contact with the sense organ is perception and nothing else; whatever manifests as immediate (aparokṣa) while the operation of the sense organ continues is perception, and such is the case with Brahminhood.
That too is perceptible, for we, with eyes wide open,

perceive it immediately upon the recognition of specific lineages among those families distinguished by various gotras and clans such as Vasiṣṭha, Kāśyapa, and Śaṭhamarṣaṇa, and who are pure in their conduct.
Manifesting Brahminhood most clearly through his shining sacred thread, upper garment, topknot, and girdle of muñja grass—
this is not at all extraordinary.
As for the claim that the sense organ apprehends Brahminhood only by depending on the connection with a specific lineage, [we reply that] in all cases,
the sense organ is assisted by the procedure consisting of place, time, physical form, and so forth.
It is the cause for the arising of the determination of its own object; it is the very nature of a mere instrument that it requires a procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
As it has been said:
"For there is no such cause in the world or in the Veda which has no desire to assist that which is to be accomplished through the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance). And thus,
by means of the eye assisted by the memory of the continuity [of the ritual procedure]...
Brahminhood, while being cognized, does not relinquish its status as an object of direct perception.
And thus it is observed that, depending on various auxiliary factors,
the eye functions as the instrument for the cognition of genus, just as has been stated.
Gold is undoubtedly distinguished from its form as copper and so forth;
likewise, melted ghee is distinguished from oil by its smell or its taste.
Fire covered by ashes is perceived through touch;
and even when the nature of a horse or the like is at a distance, certainty arises from sound.
The nature of a jar and the like is determined by its shape; that of a Brahmin and the like, by birth;
and in some cases, also by conduct, when the kingdom has been properly governed.
Thus.
It has been stated that when two lumps of flesh are observed to be identical in age and appearance, their difference does not manifest to the eye at that very moment.
The perceptibility of the separation is not negated by this much;
rather, due to the defect of similarity, there may be a non-apprehension of the separation in that case.
Since there was no immediate discernment between a mother-of-pearl shell and silver, which are identical in color and shape,
why should it not occur even at a later time?
In this way, the distinction between Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas would not be perceptible; or else, if Brahminhood were simply the state of being born from a specific lineage,
that [status] would be established through positive and negative concomitance according to worldly convention.
It must indeed be understood as being like any other action. But what are those specific qualities upon which the elders employ the word "Brāhmaṇa," and in whom do they employ it?
It has been stated many times that [the term applies] to those who possess the traditional knowledge of their lineage, ancestral seers (*ṛṣi*), and so forth.
Let the irrelevant deliberation cease; the ancient narrative is now being introduced.
"O Brahmins, they are established as Bhāgavatas because they possess [the marks of] lineage and so forth,
even though their birth is described as being in the lineage of Vaiśya-Vrātyas."
He who, by the command of the king, worships the shrines of Viṣṇu known as the Pañcamārhata is remembered as a Bhāgavata.
"From a Vaiśya, however, [a son] is born from a Vrātya"—since we observe these two statements, we ask here: what is understood from these two declarations?
Either the connection with the literal meaning must be accepted, or a restrictive rule must be stated.
First of all, it is not possible to restrict the words *sāttvata* and *bhāgavata* so that they denote only the Vaiśya and the Vrātya, because such a meaning is not perceived.

Furthermore, this would lead to an over-extension of the argument; for in the expression "the fifth is a Sātvata," there is no perception of a prohibition against the two words *sātvata* and *bhāgavata* denoting different meanings, as that would entail the abandonment of what is heard in the text and the assumption of what is not heard. For here [in the relevant passage], [the term refers to] one born from the lineage of a *vrātya* Vaiśya.

Regarding the phrase "he who is the fifth, the Sātvata," it is understood that the lineage is designated by the name "Sātvata," because the word "fifth" functions as the subject (the meaning being that it serves to establish the referent), due to its being mentioned first.

And even if the fifth [member] were a Sātvata, he would have to be a Vaiśya-vrātya as the fifth; for it is not the case that because the subject (uddiśyamāna) possesses fire, the predicate (upādīyamāna)—fire—must necessarily possess smoke. Therefore...
The status of those designated as Sātvatas and Bhāgavatas cannot be determined as being *vrātyas* based on such an examination of traditional memory (*smṛti*).
Furthermore, if it is argued that the use of these two terms is observed even for other castes (*jāti*), then—

Because they are denoted by that term [“vipro”], even for Brahmins who follow the scriptures of the Blessed One, their belonging to that same caste is certain; furthermore, because the word “ācārya,” which is recited alongside it in that very context, is observed to be used in reference to the offspring of a degraded *vrātya*.
Even for one who is devoted to the twice-born and who bestows the Vedas along with their limbs and secret doctrines, there would be the state of being a *vrātya*.

Now, although he is designated by the word "teacher" (*ācārya*), which denotes a *vrātya*, his status as a Brahmin who has not fallen from his vows is determined by another means of knowledge; thus, regarding the word "teacher"—

Since a designation is possible through the application of qualities such as "it gathers his intellect," there is no suspicion of their being *vrātyas*; for even though they are here designated by the terms *sātvata* and *bhāgavata*, which denote a distinct caste (*jātyantara*), these followers of the Lord’s scripture—
Since their Brāhmaṇahood is firmly established through the clear recollection of their specific lineage (*gotra*), *ṛṣi* ancestors, and so forth,

and since the application of the terms "Sātvata" and "Bhāgavata" is possible only through the yoga of devotion to the Lord who abounds in goodness (*sattva*), no suspicion of their being outcasts (*vrātya*) can arise; this is what is meant.
Nor does the fact that things are not denotable by the same word imply they belong to the same genus;
otherwise, because of the word "teacher" (*ācārya*), a Brāhmaṇa would have to be a frog.
[If you say: "Because it is denoted by that word, why then is a lion merely a frog?"
Likewise, because it is denotable by the word "cow," sound (śabda) is also possessed of horns;
and therefore,
[the statement] "The teacher Sudhanvan" and so forth, like those that denote other meanings, [are not definitive].
They are employed in the lineage of the Vrātyas; likewise, these two shall come to be so.

As for what was stated— that when both the powers of etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) are present, it is more appropriate to rely on the conventional power of the words *sāttvata* and *bhāgavata*— that is incorrect, since the denotation is established through the power of the etymological parts alone.
For when [the conventional meaning] exists, it is illogical to postulate an uncreated, indivisible power (of etymology).
Indeed, even he who accepts that the words *sātvata* and *bhāgavata* possess a conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakti*) with respect to a birth in the lineage of the Vaiśya-vrātyas—
He indeed accepts that, elsewhere, the base words *sattva* and *bhagavat*,
and the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix produced from them, possess the capacity to denote a different meaning, namely *sāttvata*.

Having established the rule that "by means of merit performed in other births, a man becomes a devotee of the Lord" (bhāgavata), even here [in the case of the *vrātya*], since a livelihood is possible through that very connection despite being born into a lineage of *vrātyas*, no evidence warrants the postulation of a separate power (*śakti*).

And even in the absence of direct worship of the Blessed One, it is possible for these [devotees] as well to attain the status of Sāttvatas or Bhāgavatas through the performance of activities such as cleaning the temple of Vāsudeva, offering oblations, and protecting the image.

There is the state of being denotable by the word [Vaiśya], because the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed even for a mere relationship expressed as "this belongs to that"; and it has been stated that even one born from the lineage of a Vaiśya-vrātya is fit for activities such as the purification of the temples of the Lord and so forth, as well as for the Sātvatas.
"The cleansing of the temple of the gods, the consumption of the food offering, and the protection of the image"—
thus [it says], "in this manner, worship the temples of Viṣṇu. By this, the claim that even these [Vaiṣṇavas] are outcasts (vrātyas) due to the similarity of their livelihood is also refuted.
For indeed, one set of activities consists of cleaning the temple, offering oblations, protecting the images, and so forth;

while another set of ritual cycles consists of approaching the deity, taking up the materials, sacrificing, reciting, and practicing yoga— all these being performed day after day by the devotees of the Lord (Bhāgavatas).

Just as in the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices, so too in the Jyotiṣṭoma, the activity of the carpenter consists in the fashioning and carving of vessels such as the *graha*, *camasa*, and *juhū*; whereas that of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) consists in the recitation of specific mantras, meditation upon the deities, chanting of hymns (*abhiṣṭava*), and so forth.

Nor does that much lead to a doubt regarding the common caste of those carpenters; likewise here too, there is no such doubt concerning those others who perform the purification of the temple and so forth, following the five-fold ritual established in the scriptures of the Blessed One, even though they bear the name "temple-keepers" (prāsādapālaka) and are considered low-caste (antyaja).

And so it is said: furthermore, as for what was stated regarding the etymological nature of the words *sātvata* and *bhāgavata*, [it would follow that] even in the case of the injunction "the *rathakāra* should perform the consecration," the word *rathakāra* would [apply] by virtue of its connection with the act of making a chariot (*ratha-karaṇa*).

The objection that this would entail the livelihood of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) is untenable; for in that case, it would indeed be logical [to reject the injunction], because it would entail the sublation of the spring season and other times understood from the originative injunctions (*utpattivākya*) regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), as seen in the passage:
"The Saudhanvanas are the Ṛbhus, of sun-like vision."
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting the performance of a different caste as understood from the wording of the Vedic mantras;

for even though the Rathakāra is known from Smṛti to be of a distinct caste— arising from a Māhiṣya father and a Karīṇī mother— he is nonetheless born in the natural order from a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya.

Because of the statement of Śaṅkha that "for the chariot-maker, the rites of sacrifice, the establishment of the sacred fires, and initiation are not prohibited," there is no contradiction in his eligibility even for those actions accomplished through learning;
furthermore, since the livelihood of the three higher castes from manual crafts is prohibited, [this applies] among them.

Furthermore, because the word *rathakāra* is not [ordinarily] applicable [to the class of chariot-makers], it is determined to denote a different caste; however, no such contradiction exists here. Moreover:
Since the comprehension of its own meaning is achieved through the very powers of its constituent parts as they have been established,
the author of the Sūtras rejects the notion that the whole possesses a separate measure of authority apart from its parts.

"Because of their connection with the purpose [of sprinkling] the *prokṣaṇī* waters. And therefore, those best of the twice-born by whom the Supreme Person, the Blessed One, is worshipped through the mode of goodness (*sattva*) are called Sātvatas and Bhāgavatas.
Furthermore, other Smṛtis that establish the supreme Brahminhood of the Bhāgavatas will be demonstrated later on.
As for what was further stated— that since the status of being a Brahmin is common to all, why are these people designated by the specific terms *sātvata*, *bhāgavata*, and *ekāntika* as a rule?—
the answer is that there is no fault here, just as in the case of the terms *parivrājaka* (wandering mendicant) or *nigada* (one bound in fetters).

For just as, despite the commonality of being Brāhmaṇas and the commonality of being Yajus-texts, only certain individuals are studied as "Brāhmaṇas" and only certain texts are studied as "Yajus," so too the terms "wandering mendicants" (parivrājaka) and "recitation" (nigada) are used—
let the Brāhmaṇas remain, let the wandering mendicants be brought forward; the Yajus-texts are not present here.
Just as it is said that "the *nigadas* exist, but they are not *yajus*," so too will it be here;
for there is a statement of the logical principle that the *nigadas* constitute a fourth class of mantras, or else they are *yajus* because they possess the nature of *yajus*.

Regarding that which was stated concerning the loss of Brahminhood through the consumption of food offerings and other acts performed for the sake of livelihood during the worship of deities, a rebuttal is now provided.
For Hari was not worshipped by all the Bhāgavatas for the sake of their livelihood;
indeed, many Sātvatas are seen worshipping Him even while seeking their own worldly ends.
If there are some virtuous Sātvatas who, being distressed for a livelihood,
officiate at sacrifices for the sake of their subsistence by means of highly fortunate Vaiṣṇavas;
One cannot say that their status as Brahmins is non-existent merely on that account;
for surely, one who performs the duties of an Adhvaryu priest will not fall from his caste in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
If they were not to accept [the offerings], the worship itself would become fruitless;
therefore, for the sake of accomplishing the excellence of the worship, they accept them.
At the conclusion of the worship, gold should be given to him according to one's capacity;
otherwise, the fruit of the worship would belong only to the worshipper.
This is because of the observation in the Smṛti texts such as, "A sacrifice with meager sacrificial fees destroys [the performer]," and so forth;
[it occurs] when a priest, greedy for wealth, personally initiates a request [for payment].
Indeed, it is that very act of performing the office of the *ṛtvij* priest which is here prohibited.

For example: "If they cause one who is desirous [of the office] to perform the *ṛtvij* duties, thinking, 'Perhaps they will give me [the fee], or perhaps they will choose me,' that indeed becomes for him as if it were vomited, just as food that has been eaten [and then regurgitated]."
Thus, it benefits [the giver] even when [the gift] is being relinquished;
indeed, the giving of a dakṣiṇā purified by faith is beneficial for both parties.
He who accepts what is honored should likewise give only that which is honored.
This is because of the observation of such Smṛti texts as, "Both of them go to heaven.

As for the claim that one incurs the status of a *devalaka* (a temple-priest) by worshipping deities for the sake of livelihood or by subsisting on the treasury of the gods— that too refers to the propitiation of other deities for the sake of livelihood.
This should be understood as referring to the subject of subsisting on that treasury.
And so says the venerable Vyāsa:
"He indeed would be a *devalaka* who subsists on [the worship of] Rudrākṣas and the like."
Furthermore, there is the statement of Śāṇḍilya:
"O Sage, all those who perform sacrifices for the sake of a livelihood and are devoid of initiation are traditionally known here as *karmadevalakas*."
And one should not touch them nor lie down with them after a year has passed.
Likewise: "Some are temple-priests by birth (kalpa-devalakas), while others are temple-priests by profession (karma-devalakas)."
Now, after three years, she is unfit for divine rites.

Those twice-born who, being devoid of initiation, perform what is prescribed in the ritual manuals (kalpa) for the sake of livelihood or fame, they are indeed temple-attendants (devalakas) according to the ritual texts.
Having performed the consecration according to the rules, the initiated Brahmin should have another person worship the deity if he is himself unable to perform the adoration.
Sacrificing is indeed primary [only] in this way; otherwise, it would be secondary.
"Otherwise" means by one who is uninitiated. He clarifies that very point: "By an uninitiated Brahmin, according to whatever procedure."
Action performed for the sake of livelihood is declared to be the lowest.
From the consideration of hundreds of such Smṛti texts,
it follows that for Brāhmaṇas who are devoid of the purificatory rites (*dīkṣā-saṃskāra*) established in the Pañcarātra,
performing worship and other acts for the purpose of subsisting on the divine treasury constitutes the status of an *upabrāhmaṇa* or a *devalaka*.

It is thus determined that [the Bhāgavatas] are not unrefined; as for the claim that the Bhāgavatas are unrefined because they consume what has been offered (nirmālya) and presented (nivedya), which is censured by the learned (śiṣṭa)—to that we reply:
what exactly is meant by "offered" and "presented" in the view of the Vedic scholar (śrotriya)?
If [the practice] consisted merely of offerings of flowers and boiled rice, it would not contradict the whole world;
for the world does not approve of the abandonment of flowers and boiled rice.
Even a qualified negation is not tenable because that [qualification] is unestablished;
for a cognition of a qualified object does not arise when its qualifier has not been determined, and in this case, the qualifier cannot be determined. Why is it not possible? To the extent that—

The renunciation for the sake of a deity is the qualification; have you now accepted even the Pañcarātra scripture as authoritative, such that you would acknowledge a deity in images consecrated by mantras prescribed in the Pañcarātra tantras?

With reference to that [deity], renunciation is intended as a qualification; for how could there be deityhood for that which is being propounded if its authority were not admitted, and how much less could there be the status of *nirmālya* (remnants) or *naivedya* (offered food) for what has been renounced with reference to it? Indeed, not so.

There is no such thing as a deity by birth; for your established doctrine is that whatever is understood from authoritative verbal testimony as being the recipient of the oblation is the deity in that context.

Now, if it is argued that the status of being *nirmālya* (remnant of an offering) and *nivedya* (offered food) arises because the Pañcarātrikas accept that these items have been relinquished for the sake of the deity— well then, since those very same people have also accepted the use of *nirmālya* and *nivedya* as being supremely purifying!
In that very same way, let purity be accepted.

Alternatively, if it is argued that what is actually impure was grasped by them with the notion of purity and therefore its excellence is not accepted— well then, [let us say] that what is non-divine is [grasped] through the superimposition of the notion of divinity.
Since she is "accepted by them," let it not be admitted that what is offered with her as the intended object becomes like a discarded flower (nirmālya) or an offering (nivedya).
This is what is meant:

Because the mere abandonment of things such as heaps of flowers is undesirable, and because a qualification cannot be established according to one's own system, whereas if a qualification were defined according to another system, that very other system would result in being the most purifying; therefore, in that case—
Those who accept [the authority of the scriptures] must necessarily admit the use of the remains of offerings (nirmālya) and the food presented to the deity (nivedya).
He asks: "But how can those who accept authority in that regard [admit this]?"
The remains of offerings (nirmālya) and the food presented (naivedya) must not be rejected;
for the consumption of the remains of offerings and so forth is indeed prohibited in the Tantras,
as it has been declared in the Sanatkumārīya-saṃhitā:
Whatever oblation, flower, or even fruit has been offered [to a deity] is called *nirmālya*; one should avoid it with great care.
Likewise, in another passage:
"Having thus consumed the remains of an offering (nirmālya) or even the leavings of one who is not one's guru,
one should remain for a month subsisting only on milk, constantly reciting the eight-syllabled mantra."
"Then, having drunk the *brahmakūrca*, the man becomes purified. Likewise, in the *Indrarātra*:
"One should not subsist upon the Lord of the Gods, nor should one consume the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings)."
Likewise:
"And never [should] the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*) be used for consumption. (The variant reading *na copabhogayogyāni*—“not fit for consumption”—is also found.)
Thus it is stated; likewise in another *Saṃhitā*:
"One should not eat, nor smell, nor step over the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*). Therefore, for one who has encountered such prohibitions in numerous *Saṃhitās*, [the following applies].
How can the use of *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) be accepted as purifying?
To this, it is said: Even for an object offered to the deity, its use before ten *nāḍikās* [forty-eight minutes] have passed is not censurable.
Likewise, on the night of Indra,
the wise practitioner should establish a full vessel exceeding ten nāḍīs;
for this is declared to be the conjunction of time, both by night and by day.
However, that which remains after the proper time for offering is designated as *nirmālya*;
therefore, one should cast it into water, into fire, or bury it in the ground.
To this it is replied: here, the consumption of the remains of offerings (nirmālya) and so forth is not being praised;
rather, [what is praised is] the substance employed in the rite of Pūraṇapūjā.
The discarding [of the offerings] is prescribed after the completion of ten *nāḍikās*.

Since flowers, cooked rice, and so forth, once generally offered, have fulfilled their purpose and thus ought to be removed as *nirmālya* (used remains), the completion of the ten *nāḍikās* is established as an integral part of the worship (*pūjā*).
The installation is prescribed; one should perform the full installation exceeding ten nāḍīs.

Furthermore, even by reflecting upon the established doctrines of the Tantras, [one should include] the offering of turmeric powder, food offerings (naivedya), the water from the feet (pādāmbu), and so forth.
The established doctrine of the Tantra would not be proven; where indeed are you, and where are these insignificant ones?
Alas! Your minds have been devoured by the tips of tongues that flash with but a mere fragment of knowledge.
White and black speech shines like the orb of the spotted moon;
for only those fools such as you find fault with the words of prohibition.
For when all this is served by qualified Vaiṣṇavas,
it is capable of destroying the flood of sins, just as the drinking of soma is in a sacrifice.
For others, that [remnant] is as untouchable as a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is to dogs;
as it says in the *Īśvara-saṃhitā*:
"O son, a devotee of the Blessed One is difficult to find in this world."
Even there, that state which exists in reality is indeed even more difficult to attain.

Regarding the water for washing the feet (*pādodaka*) and the offered food (*siddhānna*), as Uddhava said to the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa in the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam*: "May we, Your servants who eat the remnants of Your meal, conquer Your illusory power (*māyā*). And [the same applies] when these have been offered.
For when garlands and such are enjoyed, it is indeed for the sake of enjoyment alone.
And therefore, O Six-faced One, for those devoid of devotion and those who are not devotees,
everything that is purified by the vision of the mantra of the Lord is indeed forbidden;
thus it is stated in another section as well.
This saffron, sandalwood, and camphor unguent,
having been touched by the body of Viṣṇu, is indeed the purifier of purifiers.
Thus it is said; likewise in the *Padmodbhava*:
"Whoever bears upon his head the powder touched by the body of Viṣṇu, having obtained the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice, is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu."
Likewise, in the Īśvarasaṃhitā:
"Of everything that has been used, such as perfumes, flowers, and the like,
and of curd, milk, and so forth employed for bathing and other purposes..."
One should not employ refutations through words that produce misunderstanding— that is, those that manifest blame, envy, and so forth—
regarding those who, with the notion that she is like discarded flower-offerings (*nirmālya*), defile this goddess who is inherently purifying.
"Those fools who deny its power go to hell.

Furthermore, as for those statements which, concerning only one who has been initiated, are intent on prohibiting the use of *nirmālya* at the time of instructing him in the rules (*samaya*): [they are as follows:]
Viṣvaksena, the lord of the Blessed One’s assembly, should be understood as intent on prohibition at the time immediately following that utilization;
they should be understood with the intention of referring to the period subsequent to the utilization of the assembly place.
Since garlands, sandalwood paste, and other such offerings are first offered for the sake of the Blessed One,
they subsequently become unfit for personal use once they have been presented to Viṣvaksena.
For this very reason, the Sātvatas worship the offerings and so forth only prior to that [immersion];
therefore, that is indeed the cause of their excellence.
Moreover,
the remains of offerings made to other deities are condemned by the learned;
however, this [offering] is desired as being Vedic, like the drinking of Soma.
Indeed, those who do not accept the authority of the Blessed One’s scriptures are unable to determine whether something is called "nirmālya" (the remains of an offering).
O Blessed One, even upon investigation, it is determined by the words of all the Vedic teachers that the remains of an offering (nirmālya) is exceedingly purifying.
For when an object is based on the authority of verbal testimony, its determination must follow the word;
and it cannot be said by those who are not deaf that there is no word here.
As it is recited in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"The pure food offering (*naivedya*) of Viṣṇu is said by the sages to be fit for consumption;
having consumed any other offered food or floral remains (*nirmālya*), one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance."
The auspicious garland, which removes all sins, having been touched by the body of Viṣṇu—
whatever man wears it upon his head attains the supreme goal.

By this, it should be understood that even the traditional legal text (smṛti) stating, "Having consumed both the *nirmālya* and the *nivedya*, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance," refers specifically to [the worship of] Rudrakālī and others; likewise, in the Mahābhārata:
Meditating on Hari in his heart, being composed, he should offer the food to Him;
then, taking up a portion of the food with the middle finger, the ring finger, and the thumb.
Then, one should offer oblations in sequence with "Svāhā" to Prāṇa, and then to Apāna, Vyāna, Udāna, and Samāna.
Thus it is said; likewise in another passage:
"That which has been offered to the deity, one should give that to a celibate student (brahmacārin).
Likewise in the Mahābhārata:
In the home of that great-souled one, the foremost experts in the Pañcarātra ate first,
consuming the food previously partaken of by the Blessed One.
Thus, as the Lord Śaunaka has stated: "One should eat the *naivedya* oneself.
He who, out of atheism, reviles the *naivedya* of Viṣṇu—the purity of which is established by hundreds of such *smṛtis* and which pierces the fear of worldly existence—is a sinner.
Disregarding the words of the Smṛtis, it is only proper here to cut out his tongue.
But how can the offering (naivedya) be the means for the Prāṇāgnihotra?
That which has not been offered in sacrifice is not desired by the learned as a means for the oblation and so forth.
Nor can it be appropriate for the oblation to imply a different substance,
since the food is already obtained through desire and is what one subsists upon.
Nor can another meal be postulated for the purpose of offering it as a food-oblation (naivedya),
for the twice-born are enjoined by the Veda to eat only in the evening and in the morning.
There is no fault in this, because it prohibits eating in between [the prescribed times],
since the host of deities begins with Prāṇa.
It is heard that Viṣṇu is a subordinate [to the Lord], just like the attendants of Viṣṇu;
for just as even flowers, cooked rice, and other offerings presented to the Blessed One, when given to Viṣvaksena, do not entail any impropriety.
Just as in a sacrifice the Soma-juice remaining as the Hotṛ’s leavings serves for the purification of the Adhvaryu and others, so it will be in this case.
Moreover:
The scripture alone is the basis for the determination of what is fit to be eaten and what is unfit;
if that scripture declares this to be edible, what can we do?
Just as the performance of the obligatory and optional Agnihotra rites depends upon the ritual procedure,
so too in the Prāṇāgnihotra, the consumption of the food offering depends upon the ritual procedure.

As for what was said— that because the Bhāgavatas practice the sacraments beginning with *garbhādhāna* and ending with cremation, they are un-Brahmanical— even in that case, it is ignorance alone that is at fault, and not the fault of Your Honor, since these [practices] have come down through a lineage of succession.
Those studying the Vājasaneyi branch perform the sacraments, beginning with *garbhādhāna*, according to the path prescribed in the *Gṛhyasūtras* of Kātyāyana and others;
whereas those who, however, abandon the duties of the triple Veda (*trayīdharma*) starting from the recitation of the *Sāvitrī*...

They perform exactly the forty sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) prescribed in the *Ekāyana-śruti*; they also carry out, according to the rules, the matters declared in the *Gṛhya-sūtra* of their own *śākhā*.
(Although the *ātmanepada* ending would not apply to the root *sthā* when preceded by the prefix *anu*, one should simply read "anutiṣṭhanti" [they perform].)

Nevertheless, since the intended meaning is "those whose nature is practice" (*anuṣṭhāna-śīla*) or "those who are devoted to practice" (*anuṣṭhāna-parāyaṇa*), one should understand that according to Pāṇini’s rule *tācchīlya-vayaḥ-śaktiṣu cānaś*, the suffix *cānaś* is used here, and not the suffix *śānac*.

Those who are skillful and devoted [to their own branch] do not fall away from their status as Brahmins merely because they do not perform the rites prescribed in other branches; for otherwise, it would follow that others too would lose their Brahminhood due to the non-performance of rites enjoined by another branch, since caste (*jāti*) and lineage (*caraṇa*) [are universal].

Only those practices established according to the respective *gotras*, offices (*adhikāra*), and so forth are observed. Even though the ritual action (*karma*) is one and the same as recognized across all Vedic branches (*śākhās*), nevertheless, the duties (*dharma*) connected to distinct classes of qualified persons (*adhikārin*) are never combined, for they are mutually distinct.
Those who are eligible for the performance of rituals such as those dedicated to Indra and Agni— which serve as the means for enjoying objects like heaven and sons ordained by the three Vedas—

are distinct from those twice-born who, seeking liberation, are eligible for rituals that have the singular means of attaining the Lord as their goal, consisting of the approach to, the acquisition of, and the worship of the knowledge ordained by the Upanishads.

O Brāhmaṇas, for both of us, the non-performance of the rituals prescribed by each other's recensional branches (*śākhā*) results in the loss of Brāhmaṇahood (*abrāhmaṇya*). And just as the Ekāyana recension is of non-human origin (*apauruṣeya*), so too is the [text] of the Kāśmīras— [by the term "Kāśmīrāgama," what...]

We do not know specifically what was intended [by him], nor is the treatise devoted to establishing the authority of the Kāśmīra Āgama within our field of vision; thus, we are unable to say anything. However, having diligently acquired all of that, it will be revealed at the proper time.
Since this has been explained in detail in the *Āgamaprāmāṇya*, it is not introduced here. By this [work], [the author]—
having been born through some unknown merit in the Śrī-sampradāya, which follows the secret meaning of all the Vedas— either out of a desire to revive his disciples, or...
Whether out of a desire for gain by deluding disciples, or through ignorance of the true meaning of the scriptures, or by the weight of false pride, or for the purpose of confusing the world,
or due to a lack of faith in the words of the former teachers;
Whether due to an inability to understand their ultimate intended meaning, or because of being defiled by the impurities of the Kali age, or because of being drawn by one's own misfortune,
or because of a lack of knowledge regarding the extremely profound and hidden meanings concealed by the disputants; like...
Whether for the sake of proclaiming her own maturity as a debater, or out of a desire to refute [the opponent] in vain,

or else by all these reasons combined— according to the manner stated by the Blessed One that "the designation of Brahman is threefold as 'Oṃ Tat Sat'"— it consists of words such as "That" (Tat) which are unique to Brahman.

By forcibly superimposing the status of being a mantra for another deity upon the Gāyatrī mantra— which is the unique commencement of the Śrī Rāmāyaṇa dedicated to the Supreme Brahman, and which propitiates the Supreme Deity whose divinity is undisputed by any Vedic scholar— and thereby establishing its status as a common mantra, [he attempts to prove... his [point].
Those who advocate devotion to minor deities, or proclaim the non-essentiality of the twice-born,
or entertain the notion that [the Bhagavata mantras] are equivalent to minor mantras, are refuted;
for it is taught that the Bhāgavatas under discussion do not abandon those [twice-born], and even for those who do abandon them [they remain essential].

Since it is clearly admitted by the ancient teachers (*pūrvācāryas*)— through their teaching on *vrātyatva*— that the *gāyatrī* mantra establishes the status of being twice-born (*dvijatva*), even a child can easily perceive that those who dispute its necessity are turning away from the true meaning of the teachers.

As for the objection that because some Smṛtis state that the Gāyatrī has the Sun as its deity (ravidevatā) or Savitṛ as its deity (savitṛdevatā), it cannot be a mantra of the Blessed One— that argument is refuted by the statement: "Ravi is Sulocana, Sūrya is Savitṛ, and Ravilocana."
This is based solely on the lack of recognition of the name "Bhagavan" occurring in the verse;

for where, by the observation of a characteristic mark (liṅga) unique to Brahman, words such as "ākāśa"—which denote the elemental ether and so forth—are [understood to refer to Brahman] according to the rule: "The ether [is Brahman], because of its characteristic mark."

Since the venerable teachers maintain that [the terms] possess the status of designating the Supreme Brahman, how could there even be a suspicion of a disagreement regarding whether the words *ravi* and *savitr*, which fall within the list of names of the Blessed One, denote the Blessed One?

[This refers] to the learned. Nor is it the case that the author of the *Sahasranāma* himself stated that those names which are well-known as secondary (*gauṇa*) belong to the Great Soul (Viṣṇu), and so forth; thus, the status of being established for the Lord (*bhagavad-raḍhatva*) does not apply to those two [names], but rather [the application of] the words *ravi* and *savitṛ* to the Sun is [established] through lexicons (*kośa*) and the like.

Thus, it must be stated: how can there even be the possibility of these names being unique to the Blessed One? For by the statement "these are figurative," what is intended here is not that they designate the Blessed One through metaphorical function (*guṇavṛtti*), but rather through the power of their constituent parts (*avayavaśakti*).
Because they denote the Blessed One, words such as *ḍittha* and *kapittha*, which are included among the names of the Blessed One, are not arbitrary words; rather,
in both worldly and Vedic usage, those words [signify] that very referent.

The meaning is this: because those words have been extensively declared by the sages—who are free from the error of [literal] power (*śakti*) and devoid of the application of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—to refer to Vāsudeva, the Supreme Brahman, they are indeed denotative of Him.
For this very reason, it was stated that they are "well-known" with the intention of expressing their frequent usage.
In the expression *parigītāni*, the prefix *pari-* also reinforces the conventional status of the *sahasranāman* (thousand names).
Furthermore,
by the power of perceiving the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the function of the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*), characterized as the impeller of all cognitions—

Furthermore, the unique status of Brahman is established. Moreover, it is clearly evident that only that which is beloved is to be chosen in every way, and not that which is unlovely; thus, by being characterized by the mark of being "worthy of choice," its unique status as Brahman is established through its being the unsurpassed dearest object.

Consequently, because the seers did not grasp the [specific] characteristics [of the meters], and through the application of frequent usage, the conventional status (*rūḍhatva*) of the names was established; thus,
the fact that they have Sāvitrī and others as their deities serves as proof that they have the Supreme Brahman as their unique deity— this remaining point is perfectly sufficient.
And this has been thoroughly examined by our disciples elsewhere; thus,
those of far-reaching vision— who are engaged in clearing the path of the Vedic tradition by donning the armor for the subjugation of the ignorant— have acted accordingly.

However, since among those Bhāgavatas the bond of the threefold Vedic dharma— beginning with the recitation of the Sāvitrī— is very clearly perceived, it cannot tolerate any doubt regarding their being *vrātyas* (outcastes) or the like on account of having abandoned that [Vedic path].
Having broken his doctrine into pieces with various fabricated arguments, the disciples crushed it; such was the arrogance of those who vied with the Sātvata doctrine.
May Nāthamuni—whose threefold reality was directly perceived through the majesty of his own yoga—be victorious; he who is this very Śata, whose abode is the pair of feet of Mukunda.
May they shine forth until the end of the aeon, dispelling the ignorance of assemblies of arrogant and wicked scholars who are bewildered by the difficult path that rivals the Sātvata doctrine—
those whose intellects were expanded by the venerable Lord Nāthamuni and who have shaken off all worldly misfortune.
The faultless utterances, whose paths of prose and verse are heart-stealing due to their ever-peaceful nature—
thus concludes the *Āgamaprāmāṇya* composed by the venerable Yāmunamuni.
On the first day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, on a Friday, in the year 1957.
